skill: Selecting the correct logic relationship type for a strict physical-sequence dependency
scenario: On a warehouse foundation package, 'Excavate Pad Footing F-12' must be completely finished (base trimmed, inspected, and approved) before 'Place Footing Formwork F-12' can begin. There is no benefit to starting formwork early, and no physical way to place formwork inside an unexcavated pit.
question: Which logic relationship type should link these two activities?

options.label: A
options.text: Finish-to-Start (FS)

options.label: B
options.text: Start-to-Start (SS)

options.label: C
options.text: Finish-to-Finish (FF)

options.label: D
options.text: Start-to-Finish (SF)

explanation: Finish-to-Start is correct because the successor cannot begin in any physical sense until the predecessor is entirely complete. FS is the default and by far the most common relationship type in construction schedules, representing a clean hand-off of a completed work face.
reasoning: FS logic models a sequential hand-off: successor Early Start depends on predecessor Early Finish. Since formwork installation requires a finished, inspected excavation, no partial overlap is physically possible, which rules out SS, FF, and SF.
commonMistakes: Choosing SS with a long lag to 'simulate' FS, unnecessarily complicating logic that is inherently sequential.
Confusing FS with SF because 'the excavation finishes and then formwork starts' sounds superficially like SF's definition.
redFlags: Cannot state which relationship type is the default/most common in CPM schedules.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Under what circumstance might you legitimately add a lag to this FS relationship even though the work is fully sequential?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can extend basic relationship knowledge to lag usage (e.g., inspection or approval turnaround time).

followUpQuestions.prompt: What does a Start-to-Start relationship actually require to be true about the two activities?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Remedial check on relationship type definitions.

skill: Selecting the correct relationship type and lag for overlapping mobilization and production work
scenario: On a highway earthworks package, 'Mobilize Earthworks Fleet - Section 4' does not need to be fully complete before 'Bulk Excavation - Section 4' begins. Once the fleet has been arriving on site for about 2 days and enough equipment is operational, excavation can start while the remaining mobilization continues in parallel.
question: Which relationship best models this situation?

options.label: A
options.text: Finish-to-Start with 0 lag

options.label: B
options.text: Start-to-Start with a 2-day lag

options.label: C
options.text: Finish-to-Finish with a 2-day lag

options.label: D
options.text: Start-to-Start with 0 lag

explanation: Start-to-Start with a 2-day lag correctly ties the excavation's start to the mobilization's start (not its finish), while the lag reflects the 2-day ramp-up needed before enough equipment is available to begin cutting. FS would wrongly delay excavation until mobilization is 100% complete; FF would leave the start of excavation completely unconstrained; SS with 0 lag would allow excavation to start the same day mobilization begins, before any equipment has actually arrived.
reasoning: SS relationships model two activities that can proceed concurrently once a minimum offset of the predecessor has occurred. The lag quantifies that offset (here, 2 days of mobilization progress) rather than a full finish requirement.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to FS because it is the most familiar relationship, even when the narrative clearly describes overlap.
Using SS+0 and ignoring the stated 2-day ramp-up requirement.
redFlags: Cannot distinguish a lag on SS (offset from predecessor start) from a lag on FS (offset from predecessor finish).

followUpQuestions.prompt: If the fleet's arrival schedule slips by 3 days, what happens to excavation's Early Start?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Confirms the candidate understands SS ties the successor's start to the predecessor's actual/planned start, not a fixed date.

skill: Selecting Finish-to-Finish logic for progressively overlapping completion-linked work
scenario: On a data center fit-out, 'Fire Alarm Device Termination' proceeds zone by zone. 'Fire Alarm Testing & Commissioning' can test and sign off each zone as its terminations are completed, so the two activities run largely in parallel. The one hard rule is that commissioning cannot be declared complete until the very last device has been terminated.
question: Which relationship most accurately captures the hard constraint described (commissioning cannot finish before termination finishes)?

options.label: A
options.text: Finish-to-Finish (FF) between Termination and Commissioning

options.label: B
options.text: Finish-to-Start (FS) between Termination and Commissioning

options.label: C
options.text: Start-to-Start (SS) only, with no Finish-to-Finish link

options.label: D
options.text: Start-to-Finish (SF) between Termination and Commissioning

explanation: FF ties the successor's finish to the predecessor's finish, which is exactly the constraint described: testing/commissioning cannot complete until all devices are terminated. FS would force the two activities to be fully sequential, contradicting the described parallel working. SS alone with no finish linkage would allow commissioning to finish before termination is done, which is physically wrong.
reasoning: FF is the appropriate relationship whenever the completion of one activity is gated by the completion of another, even though both activities are actively progressing at the same time. This is common wherever inspection, testing, or closeout trails production work zone by zone.
commonMistakes: Choosing SS alone and assuming the finish dates will 'work themselves out' without an explicit FF link.
Believing overlapping work always implies SS only, and forgetting a finish-side constraint can coexist with it.
redFlags: Cannot explain why a schedule might legitimately carry both an SS and an FF relationship between the same activity pair.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Would you also add an SS relationship here? What would it control that the FF relationship does not?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding that SS and FF often work together (a ladder) rather than as alternatives.

skill: Recognizing the narrow, legitimate use case for a Start-to-Finish relationship
scenario: During project closeout, a temporary manned security patrol has been covering the site since mobilization. The client requires that the temporary patrol not be stood down until the permanent electronic Access Control & CCTV System has actually gone live, so there is continuous site security coverage with no gap.
question: Which relationship type, linking 'Access Control System Go-Live' (predecessor) to 'Temporary Security Patrol' (successor), correctly models 'the patrol's finish is controlled by the new system's start'?

options.label: A
options.text: Start-to-Finish (SF)

options.label: B
options.text: Finish-to-Start (FS)

options.label: C
options.text: Start-to-Start (SS)

options.label: D
options.text: Finish-to-Finish (FF)

explanation: This is the classic legitimate SF use case: the successor (temporary patrol) cannot finish until the predecessor (permanent system) starts, ensuring continuous coverage. SF is the rarest relationship type in construction schedules and is easy to misapply, but 'don't stop the old thing until the new thing has started' is precisely the scenario it exists for.
reasoning: SF links the predecessor's Start to the successor's Finish. Reversing predecessor/successor roles or using FS/SS/FF here would either create a coverage gap (if the patrol is allowed to finish before the new system starts) or force an unnecessary full overlap of the patrol with the entire new system's operation.
commonMistakes: Reversing the relationship into an FS from 'Temporary Patrol' to 'Access Control Go-Live', which reads naturally but reverses the actual driving logic and dependency direction.
Avoiding SF altogether and instead trying to hand-schedule the patrol's finish date manually with a constraint, losing the dynamic link if the go-live date slips.
redFlags: Cannot name any legitimate use case for SF and dismisses it as 'never correct', which is itself a red flag for shallow relationship knowledge.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why is SF generally discouraged as a default choice even though it is valid here?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate understands SF's low intuitiveness and high error rate, not just its textbook definition.

followUpQuestions.prompt: How would you add a small buffer lag to this SF relationship, and what would it represent?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Extends to practical lag usage on an unusual relationship type.

skill: Understanding that lag values on a relationship can be negative, creating a lead/overlap
question: True or False: A lag applied to a schedule relationship can be a negative value, which effectively creates a 'lead' allowing the successor to start (or finish) before the point the base relationship alone would dictate.

options.label: True
options.text: True

options.label: False
options.text: False

explanation: Lags can be positive (a delay/waiting period, e.g., concrete curing) or negative (a lead, e.g., allowing decking to start before the last bay of structural steel is fully erected). A negative lag on an FS relationship is the most common way leads are modeled, though P6 also allows negative lags on SS, FF, and SF relationships.
reasoning: In CPM/PDM math, lag is simply a signed offset applied on top of the relationship type's base date calculation. There is nothing in the underlying algorithm that restricts it to positive values.
commonMistakes: Believing 'lag' and 'lead' are two different relationship attributes rather than the same field with opposite signs.
Assuming negative lags are a P6-specific quirk rather than standard CPM/PDM behavior.
redFlags: States that negative durations or negative lags are 'never allowed in scheduling', conflating negative duration (invalid) with negative lag (valid and common).

followUpQuestions.prompt: What is a legitimate construction reason to use a negative lag, versus a reason it might be used inappropriately?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Moves from definitional recall to practical judgment about lead usage.

subcategory: Leads and Lags - FS Lag Calculation
skill: Calculating successor Early Start through a Finish-to-Start relationship with a positive lag
scenario: On a high-rise core package, 'Pour Suspended Slab - Level 12' has Early Start = Day 118 and Duration = 2 days (Day-1 inclusive convention, so Early Finish = Day 119). 'Strike Slab Formwork - Level 12' has a Finish-to-Start relationship from the pour activity with a lag of +6 days, representing the specified minimum curing period before formwork can be safely struck. Assume a 7-day working calendar for both activities (no non-working days to account for).
question: What is the Early Start of 'Strike Slab Formwork - Level 12'?
explanation: Early Finish of the pour = 118 + 2 - 1 = Day 119. With an FS relationship, the successor's Early Start is one work period after the predecessor's Early Finish, plus the lag: 119 + 1 + 6 = Day 126.
reasoning: Day-1 inclusive convention: EF = ES + Duration - 1. FS successor ES = predecessor EF + 1 + lag. Substituting: ES = 119 + 1 + 6 = 126.
commonMistakes: Adding the lag directly to Early Start instead of Early Finish (118 + 6 = 124), skipping the forward-pass step entirely.
Forgetting the '+1' day-count convention and answering Day 125.
Treating the 6-day lag as a duration to be added to the predecessor's own duration rather than as an offset before the successor starts.
redFlags: Cannot separate the predecessor's own forward-pass calculation from the lag applied on the relationship.
p6Checks: Relationships tab on the formwork strike activity - confirm the FS relationship and its Lag value.
Activities view - Early Start column, cross-checked against the predecessor's Early Finish.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If the specification instead required a minimum 7-day cure but the site works a 6-day week with Sundays off, would your answer change, and how would you find out?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate connects lag calculations to calendar assignment on the relationship or activity.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Walk through the forward pass on the predecessor alone first - what is its Early Finish?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Isolates whether the error is in the predecessor's own dates or in applying the lag.

subcategory: Leads and Lags - SS Lag Calculation
skill: Calculating successor Early Start through a Start-to-Start relationship with a positive lag
scenario: On a district cooling pipeline package, 'Open Trench - Zone B' has Early Start = Day 30. 'Lay Pipe - Zone B' has a Start-to-Start relationship from the trenching activity with a lag of +4 days, reflecting the length of open, safe trench the pipe crew needs available before it can begin following behind the excavator.
question: What is the Early Start of 'Lay Pipe - Zone B'?
explanation: For an SS relationship, the successor's Early Start is simply the predecessor's Early Start plus the lag: 30 + 4 = Day 34. The predecessor's own duration or Early Finish plays no role in an SS-only calculation.
reasoning: SS successor ES = predecessor ES + lag. Substituting: ES = 30 + 4 = 34.
commonMistakes: Using the predecessor's Early Finish instead of Early Start, confusing SS math with FS math.
Adding an extra '+1' day-count offset that only applies to FS relationships, not SS.
redFlags: Applies the same '+1' forward-pass convention to SS/FF relationships as to FS, indicating a mechanical rather than conceptual understanding of the date math.
p6Checks: Relationships tab on the pipe-laying activity to confirm SS relationship type and lag value.
Gantt chart bar overlap to visually sanity-check that pipe-laying starts partway through, not after, trenching.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If trenching's Early Start later slips to Day 33 during a progress update, what happens to pipe-laying's Early Start, and does the lag value itself change?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate understands the lag is a fixed offset that re-applies dynamically to a moving predecessor date, not a one-time calculation.

skill: Determining which of two simultaneous relationships between the same activity pair is actually driving the successor's dates
scenario: On a hyperscale data center fit-out, 'Cable Pulling - Fire Zone 3' has Early Start = Day 10 and Duration = 15 days (Early Finish = Day 24). It drives 'Termination & Testing - Fire Zone 3' through two simultaneous relationships: a Start-to-Start with a 3-day lag (the testing crew can begin terminating already-pulled cable 3 days after pulling starts) and a Finish-to-Finish with a 2-day lag (testing must not finish earlier than 2 days after all cable pulling is finished). Termination & Testing's own duration is 20 days.
question: Calculate the Early Start and Early Finish of 'Termination & Testing - Fire Zone 3'. State which of the two relationships is actually driving its dates, and describe how you would confirm this in P6.
expectedAnswer: Via SS: ES = 10 + 3 = Day 13; with its own 20-day duration, EF = 13 + 20 - 1 = Day 32. Via FF: the minimum required EF = 24 (predecessor EF) + 2 = Day 26. Since the SS-derived EF of Day 32 already exceeds the FF-required minimum of Day 26, the SS relationship is the one actually controlling the successor's dates; the FF relationship currently has slack (32 - 26 = 6 days) and is non-driving for this pair.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate explicitly checks both governing paths rather than assuming the 'later' relationship type by name always wins, and states that P6 takes the latest (most constraining) of all applicable relationship-derived dates when multiple relationships link the same pair.
expertAnswer: An expert notes that which relationship drives can flip if durations or lags change later (e.g., if Termination & Testing's duration were compressed to 12 days, the FF constraint would become binding at EF=26 instead), and recommends periodically re-checking the Driving indicator on multi-relationship pairs during progress updates rather than assuming the original governing relationship stays governing.
explanation: When two relationships link the same activity pair, the successor is scheduled at the latest (most constraining) date implied by either relationship. Here the SS path produces a later Early Finish than the FF path requires as a minimum, so SS governs.
reasoning: SS-derived EF = (predecessor ES + SS lag) + successor duration - 1 = (10+3) + 20 - 1 = 32. FF-derived minimum EF = predecessor EF + FF lag = 24 + 2 = 26. Comparing 32 to 26, the SS path is later/more constraining, so it drives.
commonMistakes: Assuming Finish-to-Finish relationships automatically dominate because they reference the 'final' completion point.
Calculating each relationship's implied date correctly but never comparing them to determine which one actually governs.
Forgetting that the SS-derived Early Finish must include the successor's own duration, not just its Early Start.
redFlags: Cannot reconcile two simultaneous relationships between the same pair and simply picks one relationship type without checking the other.
p6Checks: Relationships tab on Termination & Testing - review both relationship rows and lags.
Activities view - add the 'Driving' column or open the Relationships/Trace Logic view to confirm which specific predecessor relationship is flagged as driving.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If Termination & Testing's duration were compressed to 12 days instead of 20, would the driving relationship change? Recalculate.
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can redo the comparison with new numbers rather than having memorized the first answer.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why might a schedule intentionally carry both an SS and an FF relationship instead of just one?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding of ladder-style logic used to bound both the start and finish of overlapping work.

subcategory: Leads and Lags - Negative Lag Calculation
skill: Calculating successor Early Start through a Finish-to-Start relationship carrying a negative lag (lead)
scenario: On a distribution warehouse steel package, 'Erect Roof Structural Steel' has Early Start = Day 50 and Duration = 10 days (Early Finish = Day 59). 'Install Roof Decking' has a Finish-to-Start relationship from the erection activity carrying a lag of -3 days, modeling the fact that decking crews can follow behind and start on the earliest-completed bays 3 days before the very last steel member is erected.
question: What is the Early Start of 'Install Roof Decking'?
explanation: Even with an FS relationship, the successor's Early Start is one work period after the predecessor's Early Finish, plus the (negative) lag: 59 + 1 + (-3) = Day 57, i.e. decking starts 2 days before the steel erection's Early Finish.
reasoning: Day-1 inclusive convention: EF(pred) = 50 + 10 - 1 = 59. FS successor ES = predecessor EF + 1 + lag = 59 + 1 + (-3) = 57.
commonMistakes: Adding the lag as if it were positive, giving Day 63 instead of subtracting it.
Concluding a negative lag on FS is invalid because 'FS means fully sequential', not recognizing that a lead is exactly how overlap is modeled on an FS relationship.
redFlags: Cannot compute a negative-lag date at all, or insists negative lag values are not permitted in P6.
p6Checks: Relationships tab - confirm the Lag field accepts and displays the negative value correctly (P6 shows this as e.g. '-3').
Gantt bars - visually confirm the decking bar begins before the steel erection bar ends.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What is a more rigorous alternative to a single FS relationship with a large negative lag for modeling this kind of rolling overlap, and why might a reviewer prefer it?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate knows ladder (SS+lag / FF+lag) relationships are generally preferred over large leads on a single FS link.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What construction risk does a large negative lag on FS logic tend to hide compared to an explicit ladder relationship?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests awareness that a single FS-lead link does not constrain the rate of overlap zone by zone, unlike a true ladder.

skill: Diagnosing and resolving a circular logic (loop) error introduced during network re-sequencing
scenario: On a refinery turnaround schedule, the planner reorganizes a fragnet of 40 activities covering vessel isolation, decontamination, and re-instatement to reflect a revised work-around. Immediately after adding several new relationships and deleting others, the next scheduling run (F9) fails: P6 reports that a circular relationship exists and cannot calculate dates for a subset of activities in the fragnet, leaving their Start/Finish dates blank.
question: What would you check first to find and break the loop, and how does a loop like this typically get introduced during re-sequencing?
explanation: A logic loop occurs when a chain of relationships eventually leads back to an activity earlier in its own chain (A drives B drives C drives back to A), which makes forward/backward pass calculation impossible in that closed loop. The first move is not to guess-and-delete relationships at random, but to use P6's own loop diagnostics: P6 lists the specific activities it could not schedule due to the loop, and the Trace Logic / Relationships tab on those named activities can be walked link by link to find where the chain closes back on itself. Loops are typically introduced during re-sequencing when a predecessor relationship is added pointing 'backward' into a chain that already has a successor relationship pointing 'forward' to the same activity, often because activities were copied/pasted with their relationships and pasted into the wrong position, or because a planner added a new dependency without checking the existing downstream chain first.
reasoning: CPM's forward and backward pass are only solvable on a directed acyclic graph. Any relationship that creates a cycle makes the schedule mathematically unsolvable for that closed set of activities, which is why P6 refuses to compute dates for them rather than silently producing wrong numbers.
commonMistakes: Randomly deleting relationships on the flagged activities without first tracing which specific link closes the loop.
Assuming a loop message means widespread data corruption requiring a full schedule rebuild rather than a small, findable set of relationships.
Not checking whether the loop was introduced by a recent bulk copy/paste of activities with retained relationships.
redFlags: Cannot explain conceptually why a cycle breaks forward/backward pass math.
Has no systematic method and would only 'try things until it schedules'.
p6Checks: Read the scheduling log/error dialog for the exact activity IDs P6 could not resolve.
Open Trace Logic on one of the named activities and walk each predecessor/successor link to find where it loops back.
Check the Relationships tab for any newly added link that reverses the direction of an already-existing chain between the same two activities or their neighbors.
Re-run the schedule after removing one suspected link to confirm the loop clears, rather than removing several at once.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Once you find the loop, how do you decide which of the two conflicting relationships to remove rather than just picking one?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate reasons about which relationship reflects the true physical/contractual sequence rather than arbitrarily breaking the loop.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Could a loop ever exist in a schedule without P6 flagging an error? How would you catch it?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests awareness that P6 only catches loops within a single schedule calculation, not, for example, logic that only becomes circular after a specific out-of-sequence progress condition.

skill: Identifying and remediating open-ended (dangling) logic in a CPM network
scenario: A quality review of a 620-activity bridge-widening schedule finds 34 non-milestone activities with no predecessor and 21 non-milestone activities with no successor, excluding the single project start and finish milestones.
question: Explain why open-ended (dangling) activities like these are a schedule quality problem, what risk they create for the critical path, and how you would find and fix them in P6.
expectedAnswer: An activity with no predecessor is free to start as early as the data date allows regardless of what work actually has to happen first, and an activity with no successor cannot pull anything later even if it slips, so both understate true risk to the finish date and make the critical path unreliable. The fix is to review each flagged activity against the actual scope/sequence and add the missing logic (or confirm, for the rare legitimate exception, why none is needed).
strongAnswer: A strong candidate distinguishes dangling starts (float/risk understated because nothing forces a realistic earliest start) from dangling finishes (float overstated/downstream risk hidden because a slip here cannot propagate), and notes this is a standard schedule-quality health-check item, not just a cosmetic issue.
expertAnswer: An expert notes that open ends are especially dangerous in a schedule intended for EOT/delay-analysis purposes, since an unlinked activity cannot transmit delay through the network, understating causation in a forensic review, and recommends a standing quality gate (percentage of open-ended activities under a defined threshold) before any schedule is baselined or submitted.
explanation: Every activity other than the single project-start and project-finish milestones should normally have at least one predecessor and one successor. Missing logic breaks the chain the critical path depends on and is one of the first things reviewed in a schedule quality/health check.
reasoning: CPM's forward pass propagates dates only along existing relationships; an activity with no predecessor effectively starts 'free' at the data date/project start, and one with no successor cannot transmit its own float consumption or delay to anything downstream, so both distort the calculated critical path and float values.
commonMistakes: Treating open ends as a cosmetic filter issue rather than a substantive risk to the critical path.
Assuming any activity with float is fine to leave open-ended without checking whether the float is real or an artifact of missing logic.
Not distinguishing legitimate exceptions (e.g., a procurement activity intentionally driven only by a constraint, with justification documented) from genuine oversights.
redFlags: Cannot explain the practical CPM consequence of an open predecessor versus an open successor.
Would 'clean up' the filter by adding arbitrary logic just to make the count go to zero without checking real sequence.
p6Checks: Activities view - apply a filter for Predecessors is null/blank (excluding start milestone) and Successors is null/blank (excluding finish milestone).
Schedule Log/health-check report if available, which typically lists open-ended activity counts.
Review each flagged activity's WBS/scope against the fragnet it sits in to determine the correct missing link.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can identify genuine exceptions versus treating the metric as an absolute rule.

skill: Distinguishing genuinely redundant logic from logic that appears redundant but still adds constraint
scenario: In a commercial fit-out schedule, 'Partition Wall Framing' (A) drives 'Partition Drywall - One Side' (B) via FS+0, and B drives 'Partition Insulation & Second Side Drywall' (C) via FS+0. A schedule reviewer also finds a direct Finish-to-Start relationship from A straight to C with 0 lag.
question: Is the direct A-to-C relationship redundant? Explain how you would determine this rather than assuming it, and what you would recommend.
explanation: A direct link is only truly redundant if the date it implies for C is never later (more constraining) than the date already implied by the A-B-C path. Here, A-to-C with FS+0 implies C's Early Start = A's Early Finish + 1, while the A-B-C path implies C's Early Start = B's Early Finish + 1 (which is later, since B starts no earlier than A finishes and has its own duration). Because the A-B-C path always produces an equal-or-later date, the direct A-C link can never actually govern and is genuinely redundant here and should be removed to reduce clutter and false logic ties. This would NOT be true, and the link would NOT be redundant, if the direct A-C relationship carried a different lag or relationship type that could, under some duration/lag combination, produce a later date than the indirect path.
reasoning: A relationship is only safely called redundant after comparing the date it implies against the date implied by the alternate path(s) between the same two activities, not merely by observing that another path already exists between them. Removing a link that turns out not to be redundant would silently loosen the schedule's logic.
commonMistakes: Declaring any direct link 'redundant' purely because an indirect path also exists, without checking which path actually governs under current durations/lags.
Deleting the direct link without checking whether it carries a different lag that makes it non-redundant.
Assuming redundant logic is always harmless clutter rather than checking whether it is silently propping up an unrealistic float value.
redFlags: Cannot articulate a method for confirming redundancy beyond 'it looks like it's already covered'.
Recommends deleting logic without checking the resulting float and critical path change.
p6Checks: Compare Early Start/Finish implied by each path manually or by temporarily suspending one relationship and observing whether dates change.
Check the Relationships tab for a differing lag or relationship type on the direct link before assuming it duplicates the indirect path.
Re-run the schedule after removing the suspected redundant link and confirm float and dates are unchanged before finalizing.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can re-derive the comparison rather than having memorized 'redundant = safe to delete'.

skill: Distinguishing hard (mandatory, physically-driven) logic from soft/preferential (chosen-sequence) logic
scenario: A residential tower schedule shows 'Erect Column Formwork - Level 8' as a predecessor to 'Pour Column Concrete - Level 8' (physically impossible to pour without formwork in place). Separately, it shows 'Install Kitchen Cabinetry - Unit 8A' as a predecessor to 'Install Kitchen Cabinetry - Unit 8B' purely because the finishing contractor chose to work units in numerical order, with no physical reason 8B could not start first.
question: Which term correctly describes the second relationship (8A before 8B)?

options.label: A
options.text: Hard/mandatory logic

options.label: B
options.text: Soft/preferential (discretionary) logic

options.label: C
options.text: A resource constraint, not a logic relationship at all

options.label: D
options.text: An external constraint

explanation: Soft (preferential/discretionary) logic reflects a chosen sequence of convenience, methodology, or crew flow rather than a physical or contractual necessity. Hard logic, like formwork before pour, reflects a genuine physical impossibility of doing the work out of that order. The units-in-order example is preferential: it could be resequenced without any physical impossibility, though doing so may still have practical resourcing implications.
reasoning: The defining test for hard vs soft logic is whether the successor is physically/contractually impossible before the predecessor completes (hard), or merely a planning choice that could be changed (soft).
commonMistakes: Calling any relationship with a single crew/resource flow a 'resource constraint' rather than recognizing it is modeled as preferential logic in the network.
Assuming all logic in an approved baseline schedule must be hard logic because it was accepted by the client.
redFlags: Cannot give an example of preferential logic distinct from hard logic when asked directly.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Why does it matter to a schedule reviewer whether a critical-path-driving relationship is hard or soft logic?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate connects the concept to float credibility and resequencing flexibility, not just definitions.

skill: Computing and interpreting a schedule's logic density as a quality indicator
scenario: A logistics warehouse schedule contains 420 non-milestone activities and 751 total logic relationships (predecessor + successor ties combined). A common industry rule of thumb used in schedule health checks looks for an average of at least 2.0 relationships per activity as a rough sign of adequately-tied logic.
question: Calculate the logic density (relationships per activity) for this schedule, rounded to two decimal places.
explanation: Logic density = total relationships / total activities = 751 / 420 = 1.79. This falls below the commonly-used 2.0 rule-of-thumb threshold, suggesting the network may be under-tied (too many activities relying on only one predecessor and one successor, or worse, some open ends), which warrants a closer missing-logic review rather than an automatic conclusion of a defective schedule.
reasoning: Logic density is a simple ratio used as a quick screening indicator, not a certification of correctness; a schedule can score above 2.0 and still contain wrong logic, or score just under 2.0 and be entirely sound if activities are genuinely simple single-predecessor/single-successor items.
commonMistakes: Dividing activities by relationships instead of relationships by activities, inverting the ratio.
Treating a density above 2.0 as proof the logic is correct rather than merely well-tied in quantity.
Including milestones in the activity count when the convention being used excludes them, skewing the ratio.
redFlags: Cannot explain what the ratio is screening for beyond reciting the 2.0 number.
p6Checks: Activities view - activity count from the current filter.
Relationships/logic report or export - total relationship count.
Cross-check against the open-ends filter (SLR missing-logic review) since a low density often correlates with a higher open-end count.

skill: Designing and calculating a ladder (SS+lag / FF+lag) relationship pair to safely model rolling overlap between two crews
scenario: On a precast panel facade package, 'Erect Facade Panels - Zone D' has Early Start = Day 60 and Duration = 12 days (Early Finish = Day 71). 'Seal & Caulk Joints - Zone D' follows behind the erection crew and is linked with a ladder: a Start-to-Start relationship with a 3-day lag (sealing can begin once 3 days of panel erection have occurred) and a Finish-to-Finish relationship with a 2-day lag (sealing cannot finish until 2 days after the last panel is erected). Sealing's own duration is 10 days.
question: Calculate the Early Start and Early Finish of 'Seal & Caulk Joints - Zone D', state which relationship governs, and explain why using only the Start-to-Start relationship (without the Finish-to-Finish cap) would be a risky way to model this overlap.
expectedAnswer: SS-derived ES = 60 + 3 = Day 63; with 10-day duration, EF = 63 + 10 - 1 = Day 72. FF-derived minimum EF = 71 + 2 = Day 73. Since the FF-required minimum (73) is later than the SS-derived EF (72), the Finish-to-Finish relationship governs, pushing the actual Early Finish to Day 73 and, since duration is fixed, the Early Start back to Day 64 (73 - 10 + 1). Using only SS without the FF cap would let sealing finish on Day 72, one day before panel erection even finishes on Day 71 being sealed at all on the last panel - the FF relationship exists specifically to prevent the successor from finishing before the predecessor's own finish-linked minimum offset is respected.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate explicitly recalculates the Early Start after finding FF governs, rather than reporting only the ES from the SS relationship, and states this in general terms: a ladder relationship's actual driving link can change depending on the two activities' relative durations and lags, so both legs must always be checked.
expertAnswer: An expert notes that in this case the FF governs partly because sealing's duration (10 days) is shorter than the offset needed to cover the full erection duration properly, and recommends reviewing whether sealing's crew size/duration should be adjusted so that the SS relationship is the one governing in steady-state, with FF acting purely as a safety cap rather than the everyday driver - since a schedule where the 'safety cap' relationship is doing the actual day-to-day driving often signals the production rates of the two trades are mismatched.
explanation: A ladder relationship uses SS+lag to control when the successor can begin trailing the predecessor, and FF+lag to guarantee the successor cannot complete before an appropriate offset past the predecessor's own finish, bounding the overlap on both ends. Checking both legs and taking the later (more constraining) implied date is required to get correct dates.
reasoning: SS path: ES = 60+3=63, EF=63+10-1=72. FF path: minimum EF = 71+2=73. Since 73 > 72, FF governs: actual EF=73, and ES is backed out from the fixed 10-day duration as 73-10+1=64.
commonMistakes: Reporting only the SS-derived Early Start (63) as final without checking whether the FF relationship pushes the finish (and therefore the start) later.
Assuming SS and FF always agree and only calculating one of the two legs.
Forgetting to recompute Early Start once Early Finish is found to be governed by FF, since duration is fixed.
redFlags: Cannot explain the physical risk of using SS alone without an FF cap on trailing/overlapping trade work.
p6Checks: Relationships tab on the sealing activity - confirm both SS and FF relationships and their lags are present.
Activities view - add the Driving Relationship or open Trace Logic to confirm which of the two links is currently driving.
Gantt chart - visually confirm the sealing bar does not finish before the erection bar's FF-required offset.

subcategory: Leads and Lags - FF-Governed Start Recalculation
skill: Recognizing that a Finish-to-Finish relationship can pull a successor's Early Start later even with no start-side logic driving it
scenario: On a power substation package, 'Protection Relay Configuration' has Early Finish = Day 90. 'Relay Function Test Sign-off' is linked to it by a single Finish-to-Finish relationship with a lag of +2 days (sign-off cannot be complete until 2 days after configuration is finished). Based on its own other (start-side) logic elsewhere in the network, Relay Function Test Sign-off would otherwise be free to start as early as Day 85, and its duration is 5 days.
question: Taking the Finish-to-Finish relationship into account, what is the actual Early Start and Early Finish of 'Relay Function Test Sign-off'?
explanation: Ignoring the FF relationship, the naive Early Finish from the start-side logic alone would be 85 + 5 - 1 = Day 89. The Finish-to-Finish relationship requires a minimum Early Finish of 90 + 2 = Day 92, which is later than 89, so the FF relationship governs: the actual Early Finish becomes Day 92, and because duration is fixed at 5 days, the Early Start must be backed out to 92 - 5 + 1 = Day 88 (later than the Day 85 the start-side logic alone would have allowed).
reasoning: Naive EF from start-side logic = 85+5-1=89. FF-required minimum EF = 90+2=92. Since 92 > 89, FF governs: actual EF=92, and ES is recalculated as EF - Duration + 1 = 92-5+1=88.
commonMistakes: Reporting Early Start as Day 85 because that is what the start-side logic alone implies, without checking whether the FF relationship pushes the finish (and therefore the start) later.
Adding the FF lag to the naive Early Start instead of comparing implied Early Finish values.
Assuming an FF relationship can only affect Early Finish and never has any bearing on Early Start.
redFlags: Cannot explain how a Finish-to-Finish-only relationship can end up moving a successor's Early Start.
p6Checks: Relationships tab - confirm both the start-side predecessor(s) and the FF relationship with its lag.
Activities view - compare Early Start/Early Finish before and after adding the FF link to see the shift.
Trace Logic - confirm which relationship is flagged as driving once the schedule is calculated.

subcategory: Leads and Lags - SF Lag Calculation
skill: Calculating dates through a Start-to-Finish relationship carrying a lag
scenario: During a phased hospital wing handover, 'Permanent Chiller Plant Commissioning' (predecessor) has Early Start = Day 200. 'Temporary Chiller Rental Operation' (successor) is linked to it by a Start-to-Finish relationship with a lag of +1 day, ensuring the rental unit is not stood down until 1 day after the permanent plant's commissioning has actually started (a short overlap for handover safety).
question: What is the Early Finish of 'Temporary Chiller Rental Operation'?
explanation: In a Start-to-Finish relationship, the successor's Early Finish is derived directly from the predecessor's Early Start plus the lag: 200 + 1 = Day 201. The predecessor's own duration and Early Finish play no role in this SF-only calculation.
reasoning: SF successor EF = predecessor ES + lag. Substituting: EF = 200 + 1 = 201.
commonMistakes: Using the predecessor's Early Finish instead of Early Start, confusing SF with FF math.
Applying the '+1' day-count offset used for FS relationships, which does not apply here.
Assuming SF relationships are so rare they must be a data-entry error rather than working through the math.

Gantt chart - confirm the rental bar's finish lines up just after the permanent plant's start, not its finish.

subcategory: Leads and Lags - Risk of Negative Lag on SS
skill: Evaluating whether a negative lag on a Start-to-Start relationship is a legitimate lead or a masking of missing logic
scenario: On a metro station fit-out schedule, 'Platform Screen Door Installation' is linked to 'Platform Finishes - Tiling & Flooring' by a Start-to-Start relationship with a lag of -5 days, meaning the screen door installers are shown starting 5 days before the tiling crew starts, even though the relationship is nominally 'tiling drives screen doors'.
question: Is a negative lag on a Start-to-Start relationship technically possible in P6, and does this particular use of it make logical sense? What would you check before accepting it?
explanation: P6 does technically allow a negative lag on an SS relationship, so it is not a data-entry error in the software sense. However, a negative lag on SS means the successor is scheduled to start before the predecessor even starts, which is a strange thing to model as 'predecessor drives successor' logic - if screen door installation genuinely does not depend on tiling starting first, the relationship is likely modeling the wrong dependency altogether, or the direction/pairing of predecessor and successor has been reversed, or the -5 days is being used as a workaround to force an unrelated date rather than to represent a real physical lead.
reasoning: A lead (negative lag) makes intuitive sense when it shortens a genuine overlap implied by the base relationship - e.g., letting a successor begin a few days before its predecessor fully finishes on an FS relationship. On an SS relationship, the base relationship already allows the successor to start at the same time as the predecessor; a negative lag pushes the successor's implied start to before the predecessor's own start, which is very rarely a real physical dependency and much more often signals reversed logic, wrong relationship choice, or a constraint being simulated through lag abuse.
commonMistakes: Accepting any lag value P6 allows as automatically meaning it is logically correct.
Not checking whether the predecessor/successor roles are actually reversed from what the physical sequence requires.
Assuming negative lag is inherently wrong in all cases rather than checking the specific relationship type and direction here.
redFlags: Cannot articulate why a negative SS lag is unusual compared to a negative FS lag.
Accepts the relationship without checking whether it was meant to run the other direction.
p6Checks: Relationships tab - verify which activity is actually flagged as predecessor vs successor, since the pairing may be reversed from what the scenario intends.
Check whether a constraint on Screen Door Installation would more honestly represent the intended early-start requirement instead of a manipulated lag.
Ask the responsible engineer for the actual physical justification for a 5-day lead before tiling even begins.

subcategory: Leads and Lags - Risk of Negative Lag on FF
skill: Diagnosing an illogical schedule condition caused by a large negative lag on a Finish-to-Finish relationship
scenario: On an LNG storage tank package, 'Hydrotest Tank Shell' has Early Finish = Day 300. It drives 'Issue Mechanical Completion Certificate' through a single Finish-to-Finish relationship carrying a lag of -10 days. A reviewer notices the certificate activity's calculated Early Finish is Day 290, ten days before the hydrotest itself is even finished, and flags it as illogical given that the certificate is supposed to confirm the hydrotest passed.
question: Explain what is technically happening in the date calculation, why this particular use of a negative FF lag is a red flag rather than a legitimate lead, and what you would recommend.
explanation: Mechanically, the FF relationship with a -10 day lag sets the minimum allowed Early Finish for the certificate activity at 300 + (-10) = Day 290, which P6 will honor if nothing else pushes it later - hence the certificate shows Early Finish Day 290, before the hydrotest it is supposed to certify. This is logically indefensible: a completion certificate cannot, in reality, be issued before the test it certifies is finished. A negative FF lag here is very likely masking either a missing predecessor relationship elsewhere that should be constraining the certificate's finish to be no earlier than the hydrotest's actual finish (i.e., it should be FF+0 or a small positive lag, not -10), or an attempt to artificially pull an out-of-sequence milestone date earlier for reporting purposes.
reasoning: FF-derived minimum EF = predecessor EF + lag = 300 + (-10) = 290. Unlike a negative lag on FS (a genuine lead into overlap), a negative lag on FF for a certify-after-test relationship removes the very protection the FF relationship exists to provide, since it explicitly permits the successor to finish before the predecessor's completion point.
commonMistakes: Accepting the calculated date because the software allowed the entry, without sanity-checking it against the real-world meaning of 'certificate follows test'.
Assuming any negative lag is inherently a data-entry typo rather than examining what physical/administrative story it would need to tell to be legitimate.
Fixing the date by adding a constraint on the certificate activity instead of correcting the underlying relationship.
redFlags: Accepts the Day 290 result as correct without questioning whether a certificate can precede its own test.
Proposes a constraint patch rather than correcting the relationship lag/logic.
p6Checks: Relationships tab on the certificate activity - review the FF lag value and challenge its origin with the responsible planner.
Check whether a direct FS relationship (test complete, then certificate issued) would more honestly represent the real process than an FF with a large negative lag.
Trace Logic to confirm no other relationship is meant to be governing this activity's finish that may have been deleted in error.

skill: Defining open-ended (dangling) logic and the standard exceptions to the rule
question: In a well-constructed CPM schedule, which of the following activities is the ONLY type generally expected to legitimately have no predecessor at all?

options.label: A
options.text: The single project-start milestone

options.label: B
options.text: Any long-lead procurement activity

options.label: C
options.text: Any activity with more than 20 days of total float

options.label: D
options.text: The first activity listed in each WBS element

explanation: The project-start milestone is the one activity expected to have no predecessor, since it represents the beginning of the network. Every other activity, including long-lead procurement, should be tied to something (even if only to the project-start milestone or a defined trigger event) so that its start is logically justified rather than simply floating free from the data date.
reasoning: An open predecessor is only 'correct' at the single point where the network genuinely begins; anywhere else it represents either a genuine start-of-sequence activity that should still be tied to the project-start milestone, or a missed logic tie.
commonMistakes: Assuming procurement activities are naturally exempt from needing predecessor logic because they 'just start when ordered'.

skill: Recognizing the schedule risk of an SS-only relationship with no corresponding Finish-to-Finish cap
scenario: On a road-widening project, 'Asphalt Base Course - Section 6' is linked to 'Asphalt Wearing Course - Section 6' by a single Start-to-Start relationship with a 2-day lag, and no Finish-to-Finish relationship exists between them. Base Course has a duration of 8 days; Wearing Course, due to a separate resource-loading decision, has been given a duration of 25 days.
question: Is it possible for 'Asphalt Wearing Course' to be calculated with an Early Finish far later than a sensible reading of the physical sequence would suggest, given only this SS+2 relationship? Explain what is happening and what you would check.
explanation: Yes, this is entirely possible and is exactly the risk of using SS alone without an FF cap: because nothing ties the successor's finish to the predecessor's finish, Wearing Course's Early Finish is governed purely by its own Early Start (driven by the SS+2 lag) plus its own 25-day duration, with no upper or lower check against when Base Course itself actually finishes. If Wearing Course's duration is unrealistically long relative to Base Course, or if Base Course later finishes early or late, nothing in this logic pair will catch a resulting physical impossibility (paving the wearing course over base course that has not actually been placed yet in that location, or leaving an enormous unexplained gap). This should prompt a check for whether a Finish-to-Finish relationship (or a tightened SS+lag scheme reflecting realistic production rates) is missing.
reasoning: SS-only logic constrains the successor's start relative to the predecessor's start, but places no floor or ceiling on the successor's finish relative to the predecessor's finish; any finish-side relationship (or a hard logic check) has to be added separately if the physical sequence requires the two finishes to stay related.
commonMistakes: Assuming an SS relationship alone is sufficient to model any overlapping trade sequence, regardless of the two activities' relative durations.
Not checking whether the successor's duration is realistic in light of the predecessor's actual progress rate.
Concluding the schedule is 'fine' simply because it calculates a date, without checking whether that date is physically sensible.
redFlags: Cannot explain what an SS-only relationship fails to control compared to a full ladder.
p6Checks: Relationships tab - confirm whether any FF relationship exists between the pair; add one if the physical sequence requires the finishes to track together.
Review the resource/production-rate basis behind the 25-day Wearing Course duration against Base Course's actual pace per section.
Gantt chart - visually check whether Wearing Course's bar extends well beyond a sensible reading of Base Course's progress.

scenario: On a wastewater treatment plant package, 'Install Process Piping - Clarifier Train 2' drives 'Pressure Test Piping - Clarifier Train 2' through a single Finish-to-Finish relationship with a 3-day lag, with no Start-to-Start relationship between them. When the schedule is calculated, Pressure Test's Early Start comes back as the same day as the project data date, far earlier than any piping has actually been installed.
question: Is this outcome consistent with correct CPM math given only an FF relationship, and what practical scheduling problem does it create?
explanation: Yes, this is exactly what an FF-only relationship allows: because nothing ties the successor's start to the predecessor's start, Pressure Test's Early Start defaults to whatever its other (non-existent, in this case) start-side logic or the project's earliest possible date allows - here, the data date itself - with only its finish constrained by the FF relationship. The result is a schedule that technically calculates without error but visually and practically implies pressure testing could start before any piping exists, which is nonsensical and would mislead anyone reading the Gantt chart or using Early Start dates for resource/crew planning.
reasoning: An FF relationship constrains only the successor's Early Finish (as a minimum, offset from the predecessor's Early Finish); it says nothing about when the successor may start. Without an SS relationship or a start constraint, the successor's Early Start floats free, typically defaulting very early.
commonMistakes: Assuming the FF relationship alone is sufficient because 'the finish dates line up correctly'.
Not noticing that an unrealistically early Early Start is itself a symptom of missing logic rather than a harmless float artifact.
Fixing the symptom with a Start On or After constraint rather than adding the missing Start-to-Start relationship.
redFlags: Does not flag the unrealistically early Early Start as a logic problem at all.

skill: Explaining how relationship logic interacts with out-of-sequence progress under Retained Logic versus Progress Override
scenario: On an airport terminal MEP package, 'Install Ceiling Grid - Zone 12' has a Finish-to-Start relationship to 'Install Ceiling Tiles - Zone 12'. Because of a sequencing decision made in the field, the tiling crew actually started and progressed 40% of Ceiling Tiles before Ceiling Grid was reported 100% complete - a classic out-of-sequence progress condition at the current data date.
question: Explain how the schedule will behave differently under the Retained Logic setting versus the Progress Override setting when this update is calculated, and which you would recommend the project use as standard practice, with reasoning.
expectedAnswer: Under Retained Logic, P6 continues to honor the FS relationship for the REMAINING (unfinished) portion of Ceiling Tiles: even though 40% is already done out of sequence, the remaining work is still scheduled to resume only once Ceiling Grid is fully complete, which can produce a schedule that shows a 'gap' where tiling appears to pause even though it may not need to in reality. Under Progress Override, P6 ignores the predecessor relationship for the remainder of the out-of-sequence activity and lets the remaining work continue forward from where it left off, driven by resources/duration alone rather than by the (already partly satisfied) predecessor logic. As a general standard, Retained Logic is more common and more defensible for forensic/contractual purposes because it preserves the network's original logic intent, while Progress Override can silently erode the schedule's logic integrity over many updates, making the critical path less reliable over time; it should only be used selectively, activity by activity, with documented justification, not as a blanket project setting.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate notes this is a project-level (or in P6, potentially activity-level 'Preserve scheduled early and late dates' options) scheduling setting that should be fixed for the life of the project and disclosed to all stakeholders, since switching between Retained Logic and Progress Override mid-project on the same schedule produces inconsistent, hard-to-reconcile date history.
expertAnswer: An expert connects this to delay-analysis and claims risk: a schedule that used Progress Override throughout will have a critical path that is harder to defend in a forensic analysis because logic was overridden rather than honored, and recommends that where out-of-sequence progress is frequent, the real fix is usually to correct the underlying logic (e.g., break the activity into sub-activities so the true achievable sequence is modeled) rather than to rely on a global override setting to paper over it update after update.
explanation: Retained Logic and Progress Override are two different ways P6 resolves what should happen to the unfinished portion of an out-of-sequence activity relative to its predecessor relationship; they can produce materially different forecast dates and different critical paths from the same underlying progress data.
reasoning: Out-of-sequence progress happens whenever an activity has actual progress recorded while its predecessor is not yet complete. The two settings represent two different philosophies for resolving the contradiction this creates between 'what actually happened' and 'what the logic says should happen next', and the choice materially changes calculated dates and the critical path without changing any physical fact about the project.
commonMistakes: Treating Retained Logic and Progress Override as producing the same result, just calculated differently.
Not recognizing that this is a schedule-wide (or documented per-activity) setting that must be applied consistently, not toggled update to update.
Recommending Progress Override purely because it 'looks less delayed' without weighing the logic-integrity and forensic-credibility cost.
redFlags: Cannot describe a concrete difference in calculated dates between the two settings.
Recommends whichever setting produces the more favorable-looking schedule without technical justification.
p6Checks: Schedule Options (F9) - check which out-of-sequence setting the project is currently using.
Activities view - review activities with actual progress but incomplete predecessors for out-of-sequence flags.
Schedule log/audit trail - check whether the setting has been changed at any point in the project's update history.

skill: Deciding whether to resequence preferential logic during fast-tracking without violating any hard logic
scenario: On a mixed-use tower interior fit-out, finishes are scheduled floor by floor from Level 2 upward purely as a planning convenience (soft/preferential logic): 'Finishes - Level 2' precedes 'Finishes - Level 3' precedes 'Finishes - Level 4', and so on, with each linked FS+0 to the next, though crews and materials could physically work any floor in any order. The client now requests acceleration of Level 6 (a flagship retail floor) ahead of the others for an earlier partial opening, and asks whether this is achievable without breaking the schedule's logic.
question: As the planner, how would you respond, and what would you actually change in the network logic to accommodate this request?
expectedAnswer: Because the floor-by-floor sequence is preferential logic, not hard logic, it can legitimately be resequenced: Level 6 Finishes can be moved ahead of Levels 3-5 in the logic chain (or run in parallel with them, resourcing permitting) without violating any physical constraint, since nothing about the building physically requires finishes to proceed strictly in floor order. The planner should re-link the chain so that Level 6 is pulled forward (e.g., directly after Level 2, or in parallel with Levels 3-5 subject to crew/resource availability), update any hard logic that does genuinely apply within Level 6 itself (structural, MEP rough-in, etc. still ahead of its own finishes), and communicate the resourcing implications of running additional floors in parallel.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate explicitly checks for any hard logic hiding inside the 'floor order' chain before resequencing - for example, if Level 6 shares a single finishes crew or a shared hoist/material delivery schedule with the other floors, that is a genuine resource or logistics constraint (not physical impossibility, but a real limiting factor) that must be addressed even though it is not hard construction logic.
expertAnswer: An expert frames the answer commercially as well as technically: quantifies the resourcing/cost impact of running Level 6 in parallel or out of the original order (extra crew mobilization, hoist congestion, potential temporary works), and recommends documenting the request and the schedule impact/cost as a formal change so the acceleration is not absorbed silently as if it were free.
explanation: Preferential (soft) logic exists precisely so that it CAN be resequenced when project priorities change, unlike hard logic which reflects genuine physical or contractual necessity. The correct response distinguishes between the sequence choice (freely changeable) and any genuine constraints that happen to travel alongside it (crew capacity, material delivery, hoisting), which must be separately assessed.
reasoning: Recognizing which links in a chain are preferential versus hard is the entire basis for being able to answer 'can we do X out of order' credibly; treating all logic as equally rigid would incorrectly tell the client the request is impossible, while ignoring genuine resource constraints hiding behind the preferential sequence would incorrectly promise something undeliverable.
commonMistakes: Telling the client the request is impossible because 'the schedule shows Level 6 after Levels 3, 4, and 5', without recognizing the logic is preferential.
Simply deleting the floor-order relationships and moving Level 6 up without checking for genuine shared-resource constraints.
Failing to flag the cost/resourcing and potential change-order implications of accelerating one floor out of sequence.
redFlags: Cannot distinguish hard from soft logic well enough to answer whether the request is feasible.
Agrees to the resequencing without checking for hidden resource conflicts.

Resource assignments/loading - check for crew or hoist conflicts if Level 6 runs in parallel with adjacent floors.

skill: Determining which of three simultaneous predecessor relationships actually governs a successor's Early Start
scenario: On a shopping mall structural package, 'Pour Elevated Slab - Zone F' has three predecessor relationships: 'Erect Slab Formwork - Zone F' (Early Finish = Day 74) via FS+1; 'Place Slab Reinforcement - Zone F' (Early Finish = Day 76) via FS+0; and 'MEP Sleeves & Embeds Inspection - Zone F' (Early Start = Day 70) via SS+3.
question: Calculate the Early Start implied by each of the three relationships, state which one actually governs the pour activity's Early Start, and explain how you would confirm this in P6.
expectedAnswer: Formwork (FS+1): implied ES = 74 + 1 + 1 = Day 76. Reinforcement (FS+0): implied ES = 76 + 1 + 0 = Day 77. MEP inspection (SS+3): implied ES = 70 + 3 = Day 73. The successor's actual Early Start is the LATEST (most constraining) of the three implied dates, so Reinforcement's FS+0 relationship governs at Day 77; the other two relationships currently have slack and are non-driving.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate explicitly compares all three implied dates side by side rather than assuming the numerically largest predecessor duration or the most 'important-sounding' activity must be the driver, and notes the governing relationship can change if any of the three predecessor dates shift on a future update.
expertAnswer: An expert notes that because Reinforcement drives by only 1 day over Formwork (77 vs 76 implied) and by 4 days over the MEP inspection path, this driving relationship is fragile - a small slip in Formwork completion could make it the new driver, so both near-critical paths deserve monitoring, not just the one currently flagged as driving.
explanation: When an activity has multiple predecessor relationships, P6 schedules it at the latest (most constraining) date implied by any one of them; that relationship is the one flagged as 'Driving' in P6's relationship data.
reasoning: Formwork FS+1: 74+1+1=76. Reinforcement FS+0: 76+1+0=77. MEP SS+3: 70+3=73. The maximum of {76, 77, 73} is 77, so Reinforcement's FS+0 relationship governs.
commonMistakes: Assuming the relationship with the longest lag, or the one listed first, is automatically the driver without calculating all three.
Forgetting the '+1' day-count convention on the FS-derived dates while applying it correctly (or not at all) inconsistently across the three.
Concluding the MEP inspection is driving because it has the earliest Early Start value, confusing the predecessor's own early date with the date it implies for the successor.
redFlags: Cannot systematically compare multiple simultaneous predecessor relationships and instead picks one impressionistically.
p6Checks: Activities view - add the Driving Relationship / Driving Predecessor column, or open the Relationships tab and check the 'Driving' flag on each predecessor row.
Trace Logic - confirm the flagged driving predecessor matches the manual calculation.
Total Float on the near-driver (Formwork) path to gauge how fragile the current driving relationship is.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding that driving-relationship analysis matters for float credibility and near-critical-path monitoring, not just the immediate date.

subcategory: Leads and Lags - Calendar Basis for Lag
skill: Understanding how the calendar used to calculate relationship lag affects computed dates across differing activity calendars
scenario: On a cross-border pipeline project, 'Weld Joint Inspection - Spread 3' runs on a 5-day working calendar (Monday-Friday). It is linked to 'Coat & Wrap Joint - Spread 3' by a Finish-to-Start relationship with a 3-day lag representing a mandatory cooling/curing period after inspection before coating can begin. The project's Schedule Options currently has 'Calendar for scheduling relationship lag' set to the 5-day activity calendar rather than a 24-hour calendar.
question: Explain what this schedule option controls, and what would change about the coating activity's Early Start if the setting were switched to a 24-hour calendar instead, assuming the inspection's Early Finish falls on a Thursday.
expectedAnswer: The 'Calendar for scheduling relationship lag' option determines whether the days counted in a relationship's lag are working days on the relevant activity calendar (skipping weekends/holidays) or continuous calendar days regardless of working status. With the current 5-day-calendar setting, a 3-day lag from a Thursday finish counts three working days forward, skipping the weekend, landing coating's Early Start later in the following week than it would under a 24-hour calendar. Switching to a 24-hour calendar would count the lag in continuous calendar days including the weekend, which for a cure/cooling period that physically continues regardless of whether crews are working is usually the more realistic choice - a chemical or thermal curing process does not pause on Saturday and Sunday - so the coating activity's Early Start would generally come out earlier (or at least not later) under a 24-hour lag calendar than under the 5-day working calendar.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate gives concrete illustrative dates (e.g., inspection finishes Thursday; on a 5-day working calendar the 3-day lag consumes Friday, Monday, Tuesday, landing the successor's start midweek the following week; on a 24-hour calendar the same 3-day lag consumes Friday, Saturday, Sunday, landing the start on Monday) to make the mechanism concrete rather than only describing it abstractly.
expertAnswer: An expert notes this setting is a project-wide (or, in newer P6 versions, potentially relationship-specific) choice that should be deliberately set based on whether the physical process behind each lag continues on non-work days, and flags the risk of leaving the default setting unexamined across an entire schedule that mixes physically-continuous lags (curing, cooling, testing dwell times) with genuinely work-day-dependent lags (e.g., inspection turnaround that only happens when the inspector's office is open) - a single global setting cannot correctly serve both cases, so activity-level lag calendar assignment (where supported) or careful case-by-case review is the more rigorous approach.
explanation: P6's lag calendar option is frequently overlooked but materially changes calculated dates whenever a lag spans a weekend or holiday period, and the correct choice depends on whether the underlying real-world process the lag represents actually pauses on non-working days or not.
reasoning: A lag counted on a 5-day calendar treats Saturday/Sunday as non-consuming (the lag 'skips' them), pushing the resulting date later in real time than the same lag counted on a continuous 24-hour calendar, which consumes weekend days as part of the lag period.
commonMistakes: Assuming lag days always mean the same thing regardless of which calendar setting is applied.
Not knowing this option exists at all, and being unable to explain why two schedulers might get different dates from the same nominal '3-day lag'.
Assuming the working-calendar setting is always the 'safe default' without considering whether the physical process is calendar-day-based.
redFlags: Cannot explain any mechanism by which the same numeric lag value could produce different calculated dates.
p6Checks: Schedule Options (F9) - locate the 'Calendar for scheduling relationship lag' setting and confirm current project configuration.
Relationships tab - check the lag calendar assignment on the specific relationship if activity-level control is available.
Manually verify a sample lag calculation against the calendar to confirm the setting is behaving as expected.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate applies judgment case by case rather than picking one global answer for every lag.

followUpQuestions.prompt: How would you discover that this setting was silently affecting your dates if nobody told you to look for it?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests diagnostic instinct for a subtle, easily-overlooked schedule setting.

subcategory: Leads and Lags - Best Practice on Negative Lags
skill: Explaining why widespread negative-lag usage is treated as a schedule quality red flag and what the preferred alternative is
scenario: A schedule quality review of a 900-activity industrial plant schedule finds that 62 relationships (about 7% of all relationships) carry a negative lag, several of them exceeding -15 days on Finish-to-Start relationships. The reviewer flags this as unusually high and asks the scheduling team to explain it before the schedule is accepted as a baseline.
question: What is the most likely explanation for a schedule accumulating this many large negative lags, and why do most schedule quality guidelines treat heavy negative-lag usage as a red flag rather than simply an efficient way to model overlap?
explanation: The most likely explanation is that large negative lags on FS relationships are frequently used as a quick way to compress the schedule or force an activity's date to match a target, without doing the more rigorous work of breaking the predecessor into smaller pieces or building a proper ladder (SS+lag/FF+lag) relationship - it is fast to type '-15' into a lag field and much slower to re-sequence the network correctly, so under schedule-compression pressure, negative lags tend to accumulate as a shortcut. This is treated as a red flag because a single large negative lag on FS hides the actual rate/extent of overlap (unlike a ladder, it doesn't constrain how much of the predecessor must be done before the successor starts working on any given portion), makes float and critical-path calculations harder to audit, and is one of the most common signs of a schedule that has been artificially manipulated to hit a target date rather than genuinely re-planned.
reasoning: A ladder relationship (SS+lag with an FF+lag cap) constrains both ends of an overlap and reflects a genuine production-rate relationship between two trades; a single FS relationship with a large negative lag achieves a similar-looking date outcome but with none of that granular control, which is why reviewers treat it as a symptom of schedule manipulation or laziness rather than legitimate planning.
commonMistakes: Defending every negative lag purely because 'the total duration comes out right in the end', without addressing the loss of granular control a ladder would provide.
Assuming any negative lag automatically means fraud, rather than recognizing it can also result from time pressure and lack of rigor without necessarily being deliberately deceptive.
Not distinguishing a handful of small, well-justified negative lags from a systemic pattern of large ones, which is the actual red flag.
redFlags: Defends heavy negative-lag usage as simply an efficient modeling choice with no acknowledgment of the audit/control tradeoff.
Cannot propose ladder relationships as the more rigorous alternative.
p6Checks: Global relationship export/filter for negative lag values, sorted by magnitude, to see the scale of the pattern.
Sample a handful of the largest negative lags and check whether a ladder (SS+lag/FF+lag) would produce a similar or more defensible result.
Check whether the negative-lag relationships cluster on the critical path (suggesting deliberate date-forcing) or are scattered on non-critical work.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate understands ladder conversion is about control/credibility, not necessarily about changing the headline date.

subcategory: Leads and Lags - Excessive Lag Usage
skill: Screening a schedule for excessive lag usage as a quality indicator
scenario: A 380-activity solar farm schedule contains 540 total relationships. A schedule health-check review counts 41 relationships carrying a positive lag greater than 5 working days. Many quality-review guidelines treat lag usage above roughly 5% of total relationships as worth a closer look.
question: What percentage of this schedule's total relationships carry a lag greater than 5 working days, and does this schedule warrant closer scrutiny under the 5% guideline?
explanation: 41 / 540 = 0.0759, or 7.59%. Since this exceeds the commonly used 5% screening threshold, the schedule would warrant a closer look at its lag usage - not an automatic rejection, but a targeted review of the largest and most critical-path-relevant lags to confirm each represents a genuine physical necessity (curing, cooling, procurement lead, inspection turnaround) rather than a way to artificially adjust dates.
reasoning: Percentage = (count of long-lag relationships / total relationships) x 100 = (41/540) x 100 = 7.59%.
commonMistakes: Dividing 540 by 41 instead of 41 by 540, inverting the percentage.
Treating any result over the threshold as automatic proof of a bad schedule rather than a trigger for targeted review.
Forgetting to convert the ratio to a percentage.
redFlags: Cannot compute the basic percentage correctly.
Treats the threshold as a hard pass/fail line rather than a screening trigger.
p6Checks: Relationships export/filter for Lag > 5 (or the relevant threshold) to identify and review the specific relationships driving the count.
Cross-check whether the flagged long-lag relationships sit on or near the critical path, since those carry more schedule risk than long lags buried in high-float work.
