followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate treats the metric as a screening tool rather than an automatic verdict.

skill: Recognizing that redundant-looking logic can still carry real planning value by constraining future resequencing risk
scenario: A senior estimator reviewing a refinery revamp schedule proposes deleting a Finish-to-Start relationship directly linking 'Pressure Vessel Delivery' to 'Final Tie-in Weld', arguing it is mathematically redundant because the same date is already enforced through an intermediate chain: Delivery -> Vessel Set -> Internals Installation -> Hydrotest -> Final Tie-in Weld. Removing it, they argue, will simplify the network with zero effect on any calculated date.
question: Assuming the mathematical redundancy claim is currently true, explain why a scheduler might still legitimately choose to keep this direct relationship, and what risk removing it introduces that pure date-comparison does not reveal.
explanation: The paradox is that a relationship can be mathematically redundant TODAY under the current durations and logic of the intermediate chain, while still serving a real protective purpose: if any activity in the intermediate chain (Vessel Set, Internals Installation, or Hydrotest) is later shortened, deleted, resequenced, or fast-tracked, the direct Delivery-to-Weld link continues to guarantee that welding physically cannot be logically scheduled before the vessel has actually been delivered, even if the indirect path no longer enforces that on its own. Removing the 'redundant' link trades a small reduction in visual/network complexity for the loss of a genuine safety net against future changes to the intermediate chain - which is a real cost, not a free simplification, particularly on a long, multi-year project where the intermediate logic is likely to be edited many times before execution.
reasoning: Redundancy is a snapshot property, evaluated against the network's current state; because durations, lags, and even the existence of intermediate activities can all change over a project's life, a link that is provably non-governing now is not the same as a link that can never matter, and deleting it removes a hard-logic floor that the rest of the network might later need without anyone noticing it is gone.
commonMistakes: Accepting the 'zero effect on any calculated date' argument as the end of the analysis, without considering how the network might change over time.

Treating all redundant-looking logic the same way, without distinguishing a genuinely meaningless duplicate (e.g., an accidental double-entry of the identical FS+0 relationship) from a deliberate protective tie.
Recommending blanket deletion of anything flagged 'redundant' by a network-simplification tool without engineering judgment.
redFlags: Cannot articulate any reason to keep a currently-non-governing relationship.
Advocates removing all redundant-flagged logic automatically as a matter of schedule 'hygiene' without qualitative review.
p6Checks: Before removing any flagged redundant relationship, simulate the removal of intermediate-chain activities/relationships to see whether the direct link would then become governing.
Document (in a logic note or basis-of-schedule) why a deliberately-retained 'redundant' relationship exists, so a future reviewer does not delete it without understanding its purpose.
Distinguish true accidental duplicates (same relationship type, same lag, entered twice) from deliberate protective direct links using relationship notes/history if available.

skill: Identifying the most likely root cause of a circular logic error introduced through copy/paste of activities and relationships
scenario: A planner copies a 15-activity 'Typical Floor Fit-out' fragnet (with its internal relationships) from Level 5 and pastes it to create the Level 6 fragnet, then manually links Level 6's first activity back to Level 5's last activity to tie the two floors together. The next schedule calculation reports a loop involving several activities spanning both floors.
question: What is the most likely cause of the loop in this situation, and what specifically would you check to confirm it?
explanation: The most likely cause is that the copy/paste operation retained one or more relationships that pointed back to the ORIGINAL Level 5 activities rather than being fully re-targeted to the new Level 6 copies - for example, if one of the pasted Level 6 activities still has a leftover predecessor or successor relationship to a Level 5 activity that was not intended, combined with the new manual link from Level 5's last activity to Level 6's first activity, the network can close into a loop (Level 5 activity -> Level 6 activity via the new link -> back to a different Level 5 activity via the leftover pasted relationship -> forward again). This should be confirmed by checking each of the newly-pasted Level 6 activities' Relationships tab specifically for any predecessor or successor still pointing to a Level 5 activity ID other than the intended single tie-in point.
reasoning: Copy/paste of a fragnet with internal relationships in P6 generally re-targets internal links correctly between the copies, but errors most often occur at the boundary - a relationship that was meant to be internal to the copied set can occasionally retain its original external target, or a planner reviewing the paste quickly can miss a stray link, and this is compounded when a new manual tie-in relationship is added without first auditing the full set of relationships on the boundary activities.
commonMistakes: Assuming the loop must be caused by the newly-added manual tie-in relationship alone, without checking for a leftover stray relationship from the copy/paste itself.
Deleting the manual tie-in relationship to clear the loop without confirming the actual closing link, which may just reintroduce the problem when the tie-in is re-added.
Not checking both boundary activities (first of Level 6, last of Level 5) systematically for all their relationships, predecessor and successor.
redFlags: Proposes a fix without first identifying which specific relationship closes the loop.
p6Checks: Relationships tab on both boundary activities (Level 5's last activity and Level 6's first activity) - list every predecessor and successor, not just the ones expected.
Trace Logic starting from one of the activities named in the scheduling error message, walking forward and backward to find where the chain closes.
Compare the full relationship list of the Level 6 copy against the original Level 5 fragnet to spot any link that was not correctly re-targeted.

followUpQuestions.prompt: How would you change your copy/paste process going forward to catch this before it causes a scheduling error?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests process improvement thinking, not just one-off troubleshooting.

skill: Understanding which relationship types are meaningful when linking to or from a zero-duration milestone
scenario: A planner is deciding how to link 'Structural Steel Complete' (a zero-duration finish milestone) as a predecessor to 'Begin Roofing Works' (a normal activity). Since the milestone has no duration, its Early Start and Early Finish are the same date.
question: Which statement about linking relationships to a zero-duration milestone is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Because a milestone's start and finish dates are identical, FS and SS relationships from it produce the same result, so either can be used interchangeably

options.label: B
options.text: Milestones cannot be used as predecessors in any relationship type

options.label: C
options.text: Only Finish-to-Finish relationships are valid when the predecessor is a milestone

options.label: D
options.text: Lag values cannot be applied to relationships involving a milestone

explanation: Because a milestone's Early Start and Early Finish coincide (zero duration), an FS or SS relationship from that milestone produces the identical result for the successor, so which one is used is mostly a matter of convention (FS is more common and reads more naturally for 'once this milestone is hit, the next activity can start'). Milestones can be used as either predecessors or successors in any relationship type, and lags apply normally.
reasoning: The mathematical identity ES = EF for a zero-duration activity collapses the distinction between relationship types that reference the predecessor's start versus its finish, when that predecessor is the milestone itself.
commonMistakes: Believing FS and SS behave differently even for a zero-duration predecessor.
Assuming milestones have special relationship-type restrictions that normal activities do not.
redFlags: Cannot explain why ES=EF for a milestone collapses the FS/SS distinction.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Does the same logic apply to Finish-to-Finish versus Start-to-Finish relationships involving that same milestone as predecessor?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can extend the ES=EF reasoning consistently to all four relationship types.

skill: Classifying a set of construction relationships as hard (mandatory) versus soft (preferential) logic
scenario: A water treatment plant schedule contains the following relationship pairs: (1) 'Backfill Pipe Trench' after 'Pressure Test Pipe' (test must pass before burying it); (2) 'Paint Handrails - Building B' after 'Paint Handrails - Building A' (same crew chose to work buildings alphabetically); (3) 'Place Roof Slab' after 'Erect Roof Formwork & Rebar' (physically cannot pour without formwork/rebar in place); (4) 'Install Carpet Tiles - Floor 3' after 'Install Carpet Tiles - Floor 2' (finishing subcontractor's chosen work sequence, no physical dependency); (5) 'Energize Switchgear' after 'Complete Switchgear Factory Acceptance Test Sign-off' (contractually and physically required before energizing).
question: Select ALL of the relationship pairs listed that represent HARD (mandatory, physically/contractually necessary) logic rather than soft/preferential logic.

options.label: A
options.text: (1) Backfill Pipe Trench after Pressure Test Pipe

options.label: B
options.text: (2) Paint Handrails - Building B after Building A

options.label: C
options.text: (3) Place Roof Slab after Erect Roof Formwork & Rebar

options.label: D
options.text: (4) Install Carpet Tiles - Floor 3 after Floor 2

options.label: E
options.text: (5) Energize Switchgear after Factory Acceptance Test Sign-off

explanation: (1), (3), and (5) all represent genuine physical or contractual/safety necessity: pressure testing before burial (cannot verify pipe integrity once buried), formwork/rebar before pouring (physically impossible otherwise), and a signed-off Factory Acceptance Test before energizing high-voltage equipment (safety and contractual requirement). (2) and (4) are both sequencing choices made by a crew/subcontractor for convenience, with no physical or contractual reason the order could not be reversed or run in parallel with adequate resources.
reasoning: The classification test is whether the successor is physically or contractually impossible before the predecessor completes (hard) versus merely a chosen order of convenience that could be changed without violating any physical or contractual fact (soft/preferential).
commonMistakes: Classifying same-trade, same-crew sequences as hard logic simply because one crew genuinely can only be in one place at a time, conflating a resource constraint with true hard logic.
Missing that the Factory Acceptance Test example is hard logic for both safety and contractual reasons, not just a scheduling convention.
Selecting all five options because every relationship in an approved schedule is assumed to be equally binding.
redFlags: Cannot distinguish resource-driven sequencing choices from true physical/contractual hard logic.

followUpQuestions.prompt: For the two soft-logic examples, what would have to be true about resources for them to actually run in parallel instead of sequentially?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate connects preferential logic to resource feasibility, not just theoretical possibility.

skill: Diagnosing a missing Finish-to-Finish cap on a ladder relationship from an illogical calculated result
scenario: On a multi-span bridge deck package, 'Place Deck Concrete - Spans 1-6' has Early Start = Day 100 and Duration = 30 days (Early Finish = Day 129). 'Strip Deck Formwork - Spans 1-6' follows behind, linked only by a Start-to-Start relationship with a 5-day lag, and has its own duration of 12 days. A reviewer notices the schedule calculates Strip Deck Formwork's Early Finish as Day 116, thirteen days BEFORE deck concrete placement across all six spans is even finished.
question: Explain what logic gap is causing this physically impossible result, and what specific fix you would make.
explanation: The calculated result (Strip Deck Formwork finishing on Day 116, while Place Deck Concrete does not finish until Day 129) is a direct symptom of the missing Finish-to-Finish half of the ladder: with only an SS+5 relationship, Strip Deck Formwork's dates are driven purely by (predecessor Early Start + 5) plus its own 12-day duration = 105+12-1=116, with nothing in the logic checking that against the concrete placement's actual finish across all six spans. The fix is to add a Finish-to-Finish relationship (with an appropriate positive lag reflecting the minimum time after the LAST span's concrete is placed before formwork on the last span can be stripped, e.g., FF+7 or whatever the concrete strength/curing basis requires) so that the successor's Early Finish is correctly bounded by the predecessor's actual finish, not just its start.
reasoning: SS-derived ES = 100+5=105; naive EF=105+12-1=116, with no FF relationship to check this against the predecessor's Early Finish of 129. Physically, formwork cannot be fully stripped across all six spans before concrete has been placed across all six spans, so the missing FF cap is the root cause, not a duration or calendar error.
commonMistakes: Attempting to fix the illogical result by extending Strip Deck Formwork's duration rather than by adding the missing finish-side relationship.
Assuming the SS relationship alone was a modeling choice rather than recognizing it as an incomplete ladder.
Fixing it with a constraint (e.g., Start On or After) instead of the structurally correct fix of adding the FF relationship.
redFlags: Cannot connect the illogical Early Finish directly to the absence of an FF relationship.
Proposes a constraint-based patch rather than correcting the underlying ladder logic.
p6Checks: Relationships tab on Strip Deck Formwork - confirm only an SS relationship exists and no FF relationship is present.
Discuss with the structural engineer the minimum cure time required before formwork strip on the LAST span, to set the correct FF lag.
Re-run the schedule after adding the FF relationship and confirm the successor's Early Finish now falls on or after a sensible offset past Day 129.

followUpQuestions.prompt: After adding the FF relationship, which relationship (SS or FF) would you expect to govern the successor's dates, and why?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Extends the fix into a driving-relationship analysis, reinforcing the ladder concept.

subcategory: Logic on Summary and WBS Activities
skill: Recognizing why relationships should be built on detail activities rather than WBS summary bars or hammock activities
scenario: A junior planner, wanting to save time linking a large fragnet, links a WBS summary bar 'Level 9 - MEP Rough-In' (which simply rolls up dates from its own child activities and is not itself a schedulable activity in P6) directly to another package's activity, instead of linking to the specific last child activity that actually finishes the MEP rough-in scope.
question: Why is linking directly to a WBS summary bar problematic in P6, and what should the planner do instead?

options.label: A
options.text: WBS summary bars are not real schedulable activities and cannot be selected as predecessors/successors in P6 at all; the planner must link to the actual detail activity that finishes the relevant scope

options.label: B
options.text: It is fine and actually preferred, since it reduces the total number of relationships in the schedule

options.label: C
options.text: It is only a problem if the WBS summary spans more than one calendar

options.label: D
options.text: It is only a problem for Finish-to-Start relationships, not for Start-to-Start relationships

explanation: In P6, WBS summary bars (and similarly, LOE/hammock rollups when configured as pure summaries) are not independently-scheduled activities with their own CPM-calculated dates driven by relationships - their bars simply reflect the earliest start and latest finish of their child activities. They generally cannot be selected as a relationship predecessor/successor in the Relationships dialog at all; real logic must be built between actual detail activities, typically the specific activity that represents true completion of the relevant scope.
reasoning: Because a WBS summary bar's dates are a derived rollup rather than an independently CPM-calculated result, allowing it to be a relationship endpoint would create ambiguity about which underlying child activity is actually meant to drive or be driven, which is why P6 does not support this and forces logic onto genuine detail activities.
commonMistakes: Believing summary-level linking is a valid shortcut that simply reduces relationship count.
Not knowing which specific detail activity within the WBS actually represents true completion of that scope for linking purposes.

skill: Designing appropriate logic for a Level-of-Effort support activity so its dates track the discrete work it supports rather than being independently fixed
scenario: On a hospital expansion project, 'Site Management & Supervision' is modeled as a Level-of-Effort (LOE) activity type in P6, intended to span the entire duration of active site construction work. Currently it is given fixed Start On and Finish On constraints matching the original baseline dates, with no relationships to any other activity.
question: Explain why this is a poor way to model an LOE support activity, and how you would rebuild its logic instead.
expectedAnswer: An LOE activity is meant to automatically track the span of the discrete work it supports; giving it fixed constraints instead of relationships defeats that purpose, because as the underlying construction activities slip or accelerate during the project, the LOE activity's dates stay frozen at the original baseline and no longer reflect when supervision is actually needed. The correct approach is to tie the LOE activity's start to the earliest relevant discrete construction activity's start (typically via a Start-to-Start relationship to the first activity in the scope it supports) and its finish to the last relevant discrete activity's finish (via a Finish-to-Finish relationship, often to a dedicated 'Substantial Completion' or similar milestone representing the true end of active site work), so that it dynamically stretches or contracts with the actual construction duration on every schedule update.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate notes that P6's Level of Effort activity type is specifically designed to automatically span from its earliest predecessor's start to its latest successor's finish once given the right relationships (rather than a fixed duration), and flags that using constraints instead of relationships on an LOE-type activity effectively disables that dynamic-span behavior.
expertAnswer: An expert connects this to cost/resource-loading implications: an LOE activity like site supervision typically carries recurring cost (staff salaries, site facilities), so if it is frozen at baseline dates while the underlying work slips, resource/cost forecasts derived from it become wrong in the same direction the schedule itself is wrong, understating cost-to-complete for supervision on a delayed project - which matters directly for cost forecasting and potential prolongation cost claims.
explanation: Level of Effort activities exist specifically to automatically span whatever discrete work they support, driven by relationships to that work rather than by fixed dates; using constraints instead undermines the entire purpose of the LOE activity type.
reasoning: P6's LOE activity type recalculates its own Start and Finish based on its earliest predecessor and latest successor each time the schedule is calculated, provided it has predecessor/successor relationships to the activities defining its span; fixed constraints override this and freeze the LOE activity regardless of what happens to the work it is meant to track.
commonMistakes: Not recognizing that constraints on an LOE activity defeat its core purpose of automatically tracking supported work.
Tying the LOE activity to only a single mid-project activity instead of the true first and last activities defining its actual span.
Overlooking the cost/resource-forecasting consequence of a frozen LOE activity on a project experiencing schedule slippage.
redFlags: Cannot explain what makes the Level of Effort activity type functionally different from a normal task-dependent activity.
p6Checks: Activity Type field - confirm the activity is genuinely set to Level of Effort in P6, not just named as if it were.
Relationships tab - remove the fixed Start On/Finish On constraints and add the appropriate SS/FF relationships to the true first/last discrete activities in its scope.
Recalculate the schedule and confirm the LOE activity's bar now stretches/contracts correctly across a test date change on one of its linked activities.

skill: Synthesizing multiple logic-quality red flags into a prioritized remediation plan before a schedule is accepted as a contractual baseline
scenario: As the Planning Manager, you are reviewing a subcontractor's proposed baseline schedule for a 1,100-activity marine terminal package before accepting it contractually. An automated health check returns: logic density 1.4 relationships/activity (below the 2.0 rule-of-thumb); 68 open-ended non-milestone activities; 9% of relationships carry lags greater than 5 days; 4% carry negative lags, several exceeding -20 days on Finish-to-Start relationships on the critical path; and a 3-day negative float condition at project level caused by two Mandatory Finish constraints placed on interim activities mid-network with no documented basis.
question: As Planning Manager, how do you prioritize which of these issues to raise with the subcontractor first, what would you require before accepting this as the contractual baseline, and what risk are you protecting the project from by not simply accepting the schedule as-is because 'it calculates and shows a finish date'?
explanation: A competent response prioritizes by contractual/forensic risk rather than by which metric looks worst numerically: the undocumented Mandatory Finish constraints causing negative float are the highest priority, because mandatory constraints can silently override real logic and the resulting negative float may not reflect genuine achievable dates at all, directly undermining the schedule's usefulness for float and delay analysis; the large negative lags on the critical path are next, since they obscure the real, granular relationship between activities on the very path that matters most for schedule risk and any future delay claim; the open ends and low logic density are real but generally lower-urgency quality issues that should still be fixed before acceptance, since they can hide float and understate risk elsewhere in the network. Before accepting this as a contractual baseline, the Planning Manager should require the subcontractor to remove or properly justify the Mandatory Finish constraints (replacing them with the correct constraint type or genuine logic), convert the largest negative-lag relationships to explicit ladder logic with documented technical basis, close the majority of open ends, and resubmit with a logic-basis narrative, rather than accept a schedule that merely 'calculates a date' without those dates being credible. The risk of accepting as-is is that the baseline becomes the reference point for all future progress measurement, float erosion tracking, and any eventual delay/EOT analysis - a baseline built on manipulated or under-developed logic produces unreliable float from day one and can itself become a point of dispute later, undermining the project's ability to fairly attribute delay to either party.
reasoning: Each individual red flag is a known schedule-quality issue, but a manager-level answer must additionally weigh which issues most directly compromise the schedule's core purpose (a credible, logic-driven forecast of the critical path and float) versus which are secondary hygiene concerns, and must connect the decision to accept or reject the baseline to its long-term consequence for progress measurement and contractual/forensic credibility over the life of the project.
commonMistakes: Treating all five red flags as equally urgent rather than prioritizing by contractual/forensic impact.

Accepting the schedule because the overall project finish date 'looks reasonable', without recognizing that a manipulated network can still produce a plausible-looking headline date while being unreliable underneath.
Rejecting the schedule outright without giving the subcontractor a specific, actionable list of required corrections tied to each issue.
redFlags: Focuses only on the headline finish date and does not connect logic-quality issues to float/forensic credibility.
Would accept the baseline as-is because it technically calculates, without recognizing the long-term risk of building progress measurement and future claims on a flawed baseline.
p6Checks: Relationships export - identify and review every Mandatory constraint and every negative lag exceeding a defined threshold, focusing on critical/near-critical path first.
Open-ends filter and logic density calculation to quantify (not just qualitatively describe) the scale of the issue for the rejection/acceptance memo.
Request the subcontractor's basis-of-schedule narrative to see whether any of the flagged items were already documented and justified before assuming all are defects.

skill: Identifying the basic behavior of a Start On constraint
scenario: A planner applies a 'Start On' constraint of a specific date to 'Mobilize Site Compound', fixing it to a date agreed with the client for site handover.
question: What is the basic effect of a Start On constraint on an activity's calculated dates?

options.label: A
options.text: It fixes the activity's Early Start to the constraint date, generally overriding what predecessor logic alone would otherwise produce as the earliest possible start

options.label: B
options.text: It only affects the Late Start date and has no effect on Early Start

options.label: C
options.text: It sets a minimum float value the activity must retain

options.label: D
options.text: It has no effect unless the activity also has a predecessor relationship

explanation: A Start On constraint pins the activity's Early Start (and generally Late Start) to the specified date, which is why it is used when an activity's start must reflect an externally fixed date such as a handover date, rather than being driven purely by predecessor logic.
reasoning: Constraints override or bound what the forward/backward pass would otherwise calculate from logic alone; Start On specifically targets the start date of the activity it is applied to.
commonMistakes: Confusing Start On with a constraint that only affects the backward pass/late dates.
Believing constraints require a predecessor relationship to take effect.
redFlags: Cannot describe which of Early/Late Start a basic date constraint affects.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What happens if predecessor logic would otherwise calculate a later Early Start than the constraint date?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Sets up the distinction between Start On and the softer Start On or After constraint.

subcategory: Constraint Types - Start On or After
skill: Applying a Start On or After (SNET) constraint and understanding it only sets a floor on the early start
scenario: On a port terminal expansion, 'Install Quay Crane Rails' has predecessor logic calculating an Early Start of Day 145. The client has separately confirmed the crane rail delivery vessel cannot berth before Day 160 due to a scheduled channel dredging closure, so the planner applies a Start On or After constraint of Day 160 to the activity.
question: What will the activity's Early Start become after applying this constraint, and what would happen instead if the predecessor logic had calculated an Early Start of Day 172 rather than Day 145?
expectedAnswer: With predecessor logic giving Day 145 (earlier than the Day 160 floor), the Start On or After constraint takes over and the activity's Early Start becomes Day 160. If predecessor logic instead calculated Day 172 (later than the constraint date), the constraint would have no effect on the Early Start at all, since Start On or After only sets a minimum/floor; the later logic-driven date of Day 172 would stand.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate explicitly names this as a 'soft' constraint in the sense that it can be overridden by logic on the later side but not the earlier side, and distinguishes it clearly from a Mandatory Start, which would force Day 160 regardless of what logic says.
expertAnswer: An expert notes that because this constraint reflects a genuine external fact (vessel/channel availability) rather than a scheduling preference, it should be documented with its basis in the schedule narrative so a future reviewer does not mistake it for an arbitrary date-forcing constraint, and flags that this constraint alone does not guarantee downstream float remains realistic if the channel closure date itself is uncertain.
explanation: Start On or After (SNET) constrains only the earliest possible date the activity's Early Start may occur; if logic alone would already produce a later date, the constraint is non-binding and the logic-driven date governs.
reasoning: SNET applies as Early Start = MAX(logic-driven Early Start, constraint date). With logic date 145 and constraint 160, MAX(145,160)=160. With logic date 172 and constraint 160, MAX(172,160)=172, so the constraint has no visible effect in that case.
commonMistakes: Assuming the constraint always forces the activity to the constraint date regardless of what logic calculates.

Confusing Start On or After with Start On, which behaves differently when logic would push the date later still (Start On is generally treated as fixed in both directions unless overridden by a later predecessor push, whereas SNET is explicitly designed only as a floor).
redFlags: Cannot state the MAX-of-two-dates logic that governs a Start On or After constraint.
p6Checks: Activity Details - Constraints tab, confirm constraint type is genuinely 'Start On or After' and not 'Start On'.
Compare the activity's Early Start before and after applying the constraint to confirm the expected behavior.
Check for a documented basis (e.g., notebook/schedule narrative note) explaining why the external date was chosen.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Does applying this constraint create any float distortion elsewhere in the network?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate understands a floor constraint can consume float on the constrained activity's successors even when it isn't itself the critical driver.

dimensions.name: technicalAccuracy
dimensions.guidance: Correctly applies the MAX-of-two-dates rule in both directions of the scenario.

dimensions.name: reasoning
dimensions.guidance: Explains why the constraint is non-binding when logic already exceeds it.

subcategory: Constraint Types - Start On or Before
skill: Applying a Start On or Before (SNLT) constraint and understanding its effect on the backward pass and float
scenario: On a rail signaling package, 'Begin Possession Works - Weekend Blockade' has an Early Start of Day 88 (from predecessor logic) and a Late Start of Day 95 (from the backward pass, giving 7 days of total float). The signaling authority has confirmed that this possession-dependent activity absolutely cannot be permitted to start any later than Day 90, since possessions are booked months in advance on a fixed calendar. The planner applies a Start On or Before constraint of Day 90.
question: What happens to this activity's Late Start and Total Float after applying the constraint, and does the Early Start change?
expectedAnswer: Start On or Before constrains the LATE side of the calculation: the activity's Late Start is capped at Day 90 instead of the logic-derived Day 95, which reduces Total Float from 7 days to 3 days (Late Start 90 - Early Start 88 + 1, using the convention consistent with the rest of the schedule, or simply 90-88=2 days depending on the exact float formula convention used - the key point is that float shrinks to reflect the imposed deadline). The Early Start itself is unaffected by this constraint type, since SNLT only bounds the late/backward-pass side, not the early/forward-pass side.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate is explicit that Start On or Before can create negative float if the Early Start itself is already later than the constraint date (e.g., if Early Start had been Day 92, the float would go negative even though nothing else in the network changed), and distinguishes this clearly from Start On or After, which affects the opposite (early) side.
expertAnswer: An expert notes that using a constraint this way effectively encodes an externally imposed deadline into the CPM float calculation, which is legitimate here because the possession date genuinely cannot move, but flags that project teams should be careful not to over-apply this constraint type to activities where the deadline is merely a target rather than a genuinely fixed external fact, since doing so manufactures artificial float compression across the schedule.
explanation: Start On or Before (SNLT) constrains only the late/backward-pass side of the calculation, capping how late the activity's Late Start may be, without touching the Early Start; this directly consumes float rather than moving the Early Start.
reasoning: SNLT applies as Late Start = MIN(logic-driven Late Start, constraint date). With logic date 95 and constraint 90, MIN(95,90)=90, so Late Start becomes 90 and Total Float reduces accordingly, while Early Start (88) is untouched since this constraint type does not participate in the forward pass.
commonMistakes: Assuming the constraint changes the Early Start, confusing SNLT with a start-side floor constraint.
Not recognizing that this constraint type can push float negative if Early Start is already later than the imposed date.
Applying SNLT when what is actually needed is a deadline on the Finish rather than the Start of the activity.
redFlags: Cannot distinguish which side (early vs late pass) a given soft constraint type affects.
p6Checks: Activity Details - Constraints tab, confirm constraint type and date.
Compare Total Float before and after applying the constraint to confirm the reduction matches expectation.
Confirm with the signaling authority whether the Day 90 date applies to Start or should actually be modeled as a Finish-side limitation instead.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If Early Start were instead Day 93, what would Total Float become, and what would that mean for the project?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests the negative-float consequence of this constraint type directly.

dimensions.guidance: Explains the float reduction mechanism and negative-float risk.

skill: Identifying the basic behavior of a Finish On constraint
scenario: A planner sets a 'Finish On' constraint of a fixed date on 'Interim Milestone - Substation Ready for Energization', matching a date fixed in the interface agreement with the utility company.
question: What does a Finish On constraint fix?

options.label: A
options.text: The activity's finish date to the exact constraint date

options.label: B
options.text: Only the activity's duration, leaving the finish date to be calculated freely from logic

options.label: C
options.text: The activity's resource assignment

options.label: D
options.text: Only the successor activities' start dates, not the constrained activity itself

explanation: Finish On fixes the constrained activity's own finish date to the exact date entered, analogous to Start On but applied to the finish side, and is typically used for interface milestones or contractually fixed completion points.
reasoning: Constraints are applied directly to the activity they are set on and alter that activity's own calculated dates; Finish On specifically targets the finish date rather than duration or resources.
commonMistakes: Confusing a date constraint with a duration constraint.
Assuming the constraint's effect is only felt by successor activities rather than the constrained activity itself.
redFlags: Cannot state that a Finish On constraint acts on the activity's own finish date.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What would you use instead if the utility company's date is a not-later-than deadline rather than an exact fixed date?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Sets up the distinction with Finish On or Before.

subcategory: Constraint Types - Finish On or After
skill: Applying a Finish On or After (FNET) constraint and understanding it only sets a floor on the early finish
scenario: On a museum exhibit fit-out, 'Install Climate Control Sensors - Gallery 3' has predecessor logic calculating an Early Finish of Day 210. The exhibit design consultant confirms sensors cannot be commissioned before Day 225 because the calibration equipment is only available from that date onward (a genuine external availability constraint). The planner applies a Finish On or After constraint of Day 225.
question: What is the Early Finish after this constraint is applied, and under what condition would this constraint have no visible effect at all?
expectedAnswer: Because logic alone gives Day 210, which is earlier than the Day 225 floor, the Finish On or After constraint takes over and the Early Finish becomes Day 225. This constraint would have no visible effect if predecessor logic already calculated an Early Finish later than Day 225 (say Day 230), since Finish On or After only sets a minimum and never pulls a later logic-driven date earlier.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate notes the successor activities' Early Start would also be pushed out accordingly (since they depend on this activity's now-later Early Finish), and recommends documenting the calibration-equipment basis so the constraint is not mistaken for arbitrary date manipulation in a later schedule review.
expertAnswer: An expert flags that if the calibration equipment availability date itself is not firm, encoding it as a hard constraint risks masking a procurement/logistics risk that should instead be tracked as a risk item or a properly-logic-linked predecessor (e.g., a 'Calibration Equipment Available' milestone with its own driving logic) rather than an isolated constraint with no visible upstream cause in the network.
explanation: Finish On or After (FNET) sets only a floor on the Early Finish: the activity cannot be calculated to finish earlier than the constraint date, but a later logic-driven date is never overridden by it.
reasoning: FNET applies as Early Finish = MAX(logic-driven Early Finish, constraint date). With logic date 210 and constraint 225, MAX(210,225)=225, so Early Finish becomes 225. If logic alone already exceeded 225, the MAX function would simply return that later logic date, making the constraint non-binding.
commonMistakes: Assuming Finish On or After always forces the exact constraint date regardless of logic.

Not recognizing that this constraint would be silently non-binding once logic later overtakes it on a future schedule update, potentially masking the fact it is no longer serving its original purpose.
redFlags: Cannot state the MAX-of-two-dates rule governing this constraint type.
p6Checks: Activity Details - Constraints tab, confirm constraint type and basis note.
Compare Early Finish before/after constraint application.
Periodically re-check whether the constraint remains binding on later schedule updates as logic-driven dates evolve.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests judgment on constraint versus logic-driven modeling for external dependencies.

subcategory: Constraint Types - Finish On or Before (Deadline Use)
skill: Distinguishing a Finish On or Before constraint used as a soft deadline check from one that is actively driving negative float
scenario: On a retail fit-out programme, the contract completion date is Day 400. The planner applies a Finish On or Before constraint of Day 400 to the project finish milestone. In the current schedule update, the milestone's logic-driven Early Finish calculates to Day 385.
question: Given that logic alone already finishes 15 days ahead of the constraint date, does this Finish On or Before constraint currently have any visible effect on the schedule's calculated dates or float? Explain what would change if a delay pushed the logic-driven Early Finish to Day 408 instead.
expectedAnswer: Currently, with logic-driven Early Finish (385) earlier than the constraint date (400), the Finish On or Before constraint is not restricting the Early Finish at all - it acts purely as a deadline check/backstop and the schedule shows genuine positive float relative to that deadline. If a delay later pushed the logic-driven Early Finish to Day 408 (later than the Day 400 constraint), the constraint would then become binding on the backward pass: Late Finish would be capped at Day 400, and because Early Finish (408) is now later than Late Finish (400), the project would show negative float, correctly flagging that the contract completion date is at risk under current logic.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate distinguishes clearly between the constraint's role when it is not yet binding (a silent deadline check, doing no calculational work but present for when it is needed) versus when it becomes binding (actively driving negative float and identifying critical/near-critical paths relative to the deadline), and notes this is exactly why Finish On or Before is the standard, correct way to represent a contractual completion date in the schedule.
expertAnswer: An expert notes that because this constraint is applied only at the single project-finish milestone (rather than scattered across many intermediate activities), it correctly reflects the actual contractual obligation without artificially constraining intermediate activities, and contrasts this good practice with the common misuse of applying similar Finish On or Before constraints to numerous interim activities 'just to be safe', which manufactures artificial float compression throughout the network instead of leaving genuine float visible for risk management.
explanation: A Finish On or Before constraint at the project level is the standard, technically correct way to encode a contractual deadline into CPM float calculations: it has no effect while the project is still forecast to finish ahead of the deadline, and only becomes an active driver of (potentially negative) float once logic-driven dates threaten to exceed it.
reasoning: FNLT applies as Late Finish = MIN(logic-driven Late Finish, constraint date). While logic-driven Early Finish (385) stays below the constraint (400), the constraint is not the binding factor in the backward pass at the project level; once Early Finish (408) exceeds the constraint (400), Late Finish is capped at 400 and Total Float = Late Finish - Early Finish becomes negative (400-408 = -8, sign convention depending on formula), correctly signaling the deadline is now at risk.
commonMistakes: Assuming a constraint that currently shows no visible effect is therefore useless or wrongly applied.
Not recognizing the exact mechanism by which the same constraint transitions from dormant to actively producing negative float.
Confusing this single project-level deadline constraint with the deliberate misuse of scattering similar constraints across many intermediate activities.
redFlags: Cannot explain why a currently non-binding constraint is still correctly applied and useful.
Cannot describe the negative-float mechanism once the constraint becomes binding.

Confirm only the single project-finish milestone (not multiple interim activities) carries this deadline constraint.

subcategory: Constraint Types - As Late As Possible
skill: Recognizing the unintended consequences of applying an As Late As Possible constraint
scenario: On an office tower schedule, 'Procure Loose Furniture' has 30 days of total float under normal logic-driven scheduling (Early Start Day 300, Late Start Day 330). Wanting the activity to visually 'hug' its late dates in the Gantt chart so the team focuses effort elsewhere first, a planner applies an As Late As Possible (ALAP) constraint to it.
question: What does the ALAP constraint actually do to this activity's dates, and what practical risk does it introduce compared to simply leaving the activity with its calculated float?
expectedAnswer: ALAP schedules the activity as late as it can be without delaying any successor activity, which pushes its Early Start to effectively equal its Late Start (using up essentially all its free float), so the activity now shows Early Start = Late Start = Day 330 with Total Float driven toward zero on that activity specifically, even though nothing about the underlying risk to the project actually changed. The practical risk is that ALAP-constrained activities appear on Total Float and near-critical-path reports as if they were genuinely critical or near-critical, when in reality they still have the same schedule risk profile as before (30 days of buffer) - just relabeled and pushed to the last responsible moment by a constraint rather than by genuine logic, which can mislead anyone reviewing the critical path or near-critical activities without checking which activities carry an ALAP constraint.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate explicitly notes ALAP consumes free float in particular (pushing to the latest point that does not delay any successor) and flags that if procurement lead times are underestimated, an ALAP-constrained activity with its float artificially zeroed out is now much closer to becoming genuinely critical with almost no cushion for real-world delivery slippage, which is a real practical risk of using it purely for visual/reporting convenience.
expertAnswer: An expert connects this to resource leveling practice: ALAP is a legitimate tool specifically intended for use during resource leveling to delay non-critical, resource-constrained work into available capacity windows, but recommends it be removed (or carefully reviewed) once leveling is complete and the schedule moves into execution, since carrying ALAP constraints through the live project execution phase compresses real buffer without any corresponding reduction in actual risk.
explanation: As Late As Possible schedules the activity at the latest point that does not push out any successor, effectively consuming its own free float and making it appear to have little or no slack on standard float reports, without changing anything about the underlying risk the float was protecting against.
reasoning: ALAP recalculates Early Start = Late Start (or as close as free float allows) rather than the normal forward-pass-driven Early Start; the activity's genuine schedule risk (how much real buffer exists before it could delay something) is unchanged, but the reported float metric that is supposed to reflect that risk is compressed to near zero, creating a mismatch between reported float and actual risk.
commonMistakes: Believing ALAP is purely a cosmetic/reporting tool with no real scheduling consequence.
Not recognizing that ALAP-driven near-zero float can be mistaken for genuine criticality by anyone reviewing float reports without checking for the constraint.
Applying ALAP broadly outside of a deliberate resource-leveling exercise, as a convenience, without understanding the float-masking side effect.
redFlags: Cannot explain that ALAP consumes float rather than simply being a visual/reporting preference with no numeric consequence.

skill: Explaining why Mandatory Start constraints can silently break the logic-driven integrity of a CPM network
scenario: On a semiconductor fab clean-room package, 'Install Cleanroom Wall Panels - Bay 4' has a Finish-to-Start predecessor relationship from 'HVAC Rough-In Inspection - Bay 4' (predecessor Early Finish = Day 220). A planner, wanting to lock the wall panel activity to a specific vendor-confirmed installation date, applies a Mandatory Start constraint of Day 210 to it - ten days BEFORE the predecessor inspection is even scheduled to finish.
question: Explain what P6 will actually calculate for this activity given the Mandatory Start constraint, why this is dangerous even though the schedule will still calculate without an error message, and what you would recommend instead.
explanation: Because a Mandatory Start constraint overrides predecessor logic entirely rather than merely bounding it, P6 will schedule Install Cleanroom Wall Panels to start exactly on Day 210 regardless of the fact that its predecessor (HVAC Rough-In Inspection) does not finish until Day 220 - the schedule will calculate cleanly, with no loop or error, but will silently show wall panel installation starting before the inspection that is supposed to precede it is even complete, which is physically nonsensical and easy to miss because P6 does not flag Mandatory constraints as a logic violation the way it treats some other conditions. This is dangerous precisely because it looks like a normal, valid, calculated schedule to anyone who does not specifically check for Mandatory constraints on the network, which makes it a favored (deliberate or accidental) way to hide a genuinely undeliverable sequence behind an apparently clean schedule. The recommendation is to replace the Mandatory Start with a Start On or After constraint (which would still respect the Day 220 predecessor finish as a genuine floor, only becoming binding if it were later than the logic-driven date) or, if the vendor date is a genuine hard requirement, to resolve the actual conflict between the inspection date and the vendor date rather than papering over it with a constraint that breaks logic silently.
reasoning: Mandatory Start (and Mandatory Finish) are the one constraint category that ignores predecessor and successor relationships entirely when calculating the constrained activity's own date, unlike every other constraint type, which at minimum still respects logic pushing the date later (even if it can force an earlier date than logic in some cases) - Mandatory constraints break that integrity completely and calculate to the exact date no matter what logic says, and P6 does not surface this as an error.
commonMistakes: Believing all constraint types respect predecessor logic in the same way and that Mandatory Start simply means 'a stronger version' of Start On.
Not recognizing that the schedule calculating without an error message does not mean the result is logically sound.
Fixing the visible symptom (moving the constraint date later) without addressing the deeper practice risk of using Mandatory constraints at all in a live network.
redFlags: Cannot explain why Mandatory Start is fundamentally different in kind (not just degree) from Start On or Start On or After.
Treats the clean schedule calculation as proof the network has no problem.
p6Checks: Global filter for all Mandatory Start and Mandatory Finish constraints in the schedule as a standard quality-review step.
For each one found, manually verify the constrained activity's predecessor logic is actually consistent with the constraint date.
Review whether a softer constraint type (SNET, SNLT, FNET, FNLT) would achieve the planner's real intent without breaking logic integrity.

skill: Explaining how a Mandatory Finish constraint can suppress genuine negative float and mislead a project team about true schedule risk
scenario: On a stadium roof structure package, the project finish milestone shows 0 days of Total Float and an on-time forecast, which the project director cites approvingly in a monthly report. During a schedule audit, you discover the finish milestone carries a Mandatory Finish constraint set to the original contract date, while multiple structural steel activities feeding into it are currently forecast, by logic alone, to finish 18 days later than that same date.
question: Explain how the schedule can show 0 float and an on-time finish at the milestone while genuine logic-driven activities feeding it are 18 days late, and what the project director's report is actually missing.
explanation: A Mandatory Finish constraint forces the milestone's own Early Finish AND Late Finish to the exact constraint date regardless of what its predecessor logic calculates, which means the milestone's displayed Total Float of 0 is an artifact of the constraint overriding logic, not a genuine reflection of the project's real schedule position - the 18-day gap between what logic-driven structural steel activities actually calculate and what the milestone is forced to show has not been resolved, it has simply been hidden from the float calculation at that single point. The project director's report is missing the fact that the true, logic-driven forecast (ignoring the Mandatory Finish override) shows the project 18 days behind the contract date; citing 0 float at the milestone as evidence of being on track is technically true of that one constrained data point but substantively misleading about the project's actual position, since Mandatory constraints do not resolve schedule conflicts, they merely stop the software from reporting them at that location.
reasoning: Because Mandatory Finish ignores predecessor logic when setting both the Early and Late Finish of the constrained activity, any genuine delay accumulating on the paths feeding into it is prevented from propagating into that activity's own float calculation - the delay is real (evidenced by the 18-day gap in the feeding activities) but it is architecturally blocked from surfacing as negative float at the one point (the project milestone) where senior stakeholders are most likely to be looking.
commonMistakes: Accepting the reported 0 float at face value because 'that's what the schedule shows'.
Not tracing back from the milestone into its feeding activities to check whether logic-driven dates are actually consistent with the constrained date.
Assuming the fix is simply to remove the constraint without also addressing the real 18-day schedule gap it was concealing.

skill: Understanding how P6's primary and secondary constraint fields combine on a single activity
scenario: A planner needs 'Deliver & Install Transformer - Substation 2' to not start before Day 250 (transformer delivery cannot arrive earlier) but also, if predecessor logic would push it later than Day 250, wants to cap how late it can be scheduled to protect a downstream energization date, without breaking predecessor logic outright the way a Mandatory constraint would. They set the Primary Constraint to Start On or After (Day 250) and the Secondary Constraint to Start On or Before (Day 265).
question: What is the effect of combining these two constraints on the same activity?

options.label: A
options.text: The activity's Early Start is floored at Day 250 by the primary constraint, and its Late Start is capped at Day 265 by the secondary constraint, together bounding the activity's start within that window while both remain soft (logic-respecting) constraints

options.label: B
options.text: Only the primary constraint has any effect; the secondary constraint is stored but never used in date calculation

options.label: C
options.text: P6 will reject this combination because two constraints cannot be applied to the same activity

options.label: D
options.text: The secondary constraint overrides and replaces the primary constraint entirely

explanation: P6 allows a Primary and a Secondary constraint on the same activity (except when the primary is Mandatory, which disables the secondary field). Here, the Start On or After primary constraint sets a floor on the Early Start, while the Start On or Before secondary constraint sets a cap on the Late Start, together creating a defined window within which the activity can be scheduled while both constraints still respect the underlying logic-driven dates outside that window.
reasoning: Primary and secondary constraints are evaluated independently on their respective sides of the CPM calculation (the primary here governs the forward pass floor, the secondary the backward pass cap), and combining a floor-type and a cap-type constraint is a standard, deliberate technique to bound an activity's date range without resorting to a Mandatory constraint.
commonMistakes: Believing only one constraint field can ever be populated per activity.
Assuming the secondary constraint is purely cosmetic/informational rather than actively participating in date calculation.
Not realizing this combination is unavailable when the primary constraint is Mandatory Start or Mandatory Finish.
redFlags: Cannot explain what a secondary constraint field is for at all.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests knowledge of the P6-specific rule disabling secondary constraints under a Mandatory primary.

skill: Calculating the negative float created by a Finish On or Before constraint that is tighter than the logic-driven finish
scenario: On a desalination plant package, 'Commission Reverse Osmosis Train 2' has a logic-driven Early Finish of Day 512. A Finish On or Before constraint of Day 498 has been applied to reflect a fixed regulatory water-testing window that cannot be missed.
question: What is the resulting Total Float (in days) on this activity's finish, given the constraint caps Late Finish at Day 498 while Early Finish remains 512?
explanation: Total Float = Late Finish - Early Finish = 498 - 512 = -14 days. The Finish On or Before constraint caps the Late Finish at Day 498, but cannot pull the logic-driven Early Finish (512) earlier, so the activity shows 14 days of negative float, correctly signaling that current logic cannot meet the regulatory testing window.
reasoning: FNLT sets Late Finish = MIN(logic-driven Late Finish, constraint date) = MIN(whatever logic gives, 498) = 498 in this case since the constraint is tighter. With Early Finish fixed at 512 by logic, Total Float = 498 - 512 = -14.
commonMistakes: Subtracting in the wrong order (512-498=14) and reporting positive float instead of negative.
Assuming the constraint pulls the Early Finish earlier to meet the deadline, rather than understanding negative float is how CPM flags the conflict instead of silently resolving it.
Reporting 0 float, not recognizing the deadline is actually already breached under current logic.
redFlags: Cannot compute Total Float from Late Finish minus Early Finish correctly, or does not recognize negative float as a valid, meaningful result.
p6Checks: Activity Details - Dates tab, compare Early Finish and Late Finish directly.
Total Float column in Activities view to confirm the negative value.
Trace back through predecessor logic to identify which upstream activities are consuming the 14 days that would need to be recovered.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Does this -14 days of float mean the whole project is 14 days behind, or only this specific path?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate understands negative float is path-specific relative to its governing constraint, not automatically a project-wide figure.

skill: Calculating downstream float consumption caused by a Start On or After constraint that delays an activity past its logic-driven early date
scenario: On a manufacturing plant expansion, 'Install Overhead Crane Rails - Bay C' has a logic-driven Early Start of Day 140 and a Late Start (from the backward pass, before any constraint) of Day 155, giving 15 days of Total Float. A Start On or After constraint of Day 152 is applied because the crane manufacturer's structural certification is not issued until that date.
question: What is the activity's Total Float after this constraint is applied?
explanation: The Start On or After constraint raises the Early Start from 140 to 152 (since 152 is later than the logic-driven 140), while the Late Start remains 155 (unaffected by this constraint type, which only bounds the early side). Total Float = Late Start - Early Start = 155 - 152 = 3 days, a reduction from the original 15 days.
reasoning: SNET sets Early Start = MAX(logic-driven Early Start, constraint date) = MAX(140, 152) = 152. Late Start is untouched by this constraint type and remains 155. Total Float = 155 - 152 = 3.
commonMistakes: Assuming Total Float is unaffected because 'the constraint only sets a floor, not a hard date'.
Forgetting to also recalculate Late Start on any successors that were themselves not independently constrained, understating the ripple effect through the network.
Computing float as Late Start minus the ORIGINAL Early Start (155-140=15) instead of the new constrained Early Start.
redFlags: Does not recognize that a floor-type constraint can still meaningfully consume float even though it never behaves like a Mandatory Start.
p6Checks: Activity Details - Dates tab, compare Early Start before and after the constraint is applied.
Total Float column to confirm the reduction from 15 to 3 days.
Check successor activities for similar float reduction propagating downstream from this constrained activity.

subcategory: Appropriate vs Abusive Use of Constraints
skill: Recognizing and responding to systemic misuse of Mandatory constraints to artificially lock a baseline schedule
scenario: You are reviewing a 2,400-activity EPC schedule ahead of monthly submission to the client. You discover that 340 activities (roughly 14%) carry Mandatory Start or Mandatory Finish constraints, all set to match the original approved baseline dates exactly. The scheduling lead explains this was done deliberately so that 'the schedule always shows the baseline plan and doesn't drift around every month', making it easier to present a stable-looking programme to the client.
question: As the reviewing planning lead, what is your concern with this practice, and what would you require the scheduling lead to change before you approve this month's submission?
explanation: Applying Mandatory constraints across 14% of activities to lock them to baseline dates defeats the entire purpose of a logic-driven CPM update: because Mandatory constraints ignore predecessor and successor logic, this practice means the schedule is no longer genuinely forecasting anything for those 340 activities - it is displaying a fixed, unchanging picture regardless of actual progress, delays, or resequencing elsewhere in the network, and float/critical-path calculations flowing through or around those activities are now unreliable. This is a serious quality and, potentially, integrity concern: presenting a 'stable-looking' schedule that is artificially locked rather than genuinely on track misrepresents the project's actual status to the client and to the project's own management, and if a delay dispute ever arises, a schedule built this way will not withstand forensic scrutiny since its dates were forced rather than calculated. The reviewer should require the scheduling lead to remove the Mandatory constraints from all 340 activities, replace genuine forecast needs with appropriate soft constraints (SNET/FNET) only where a real external basis exists, and allow the schedule to calculate honestly from logic and actual progress, even if that means presenting genuine variance to the client rather than a falsely stable picture - variance explained honestly is a normal, expected part of monthly reporting, not a failure to be hidden.
reasoning: The scheduling lead's stated goal (a stable, non-drifting presentation) is being achieved by breaking the schedule's core function (a logic-driven, honest forecast), which is the wrong trade-off; a CPM schedule that has been forced to always show baseline dates cannot simultaneously be used as a genuine progress and forecasting tool, and misrepresenting status this way carries real reputational, contractual, and potentially claims-related risk.
commonMistakes: Accepting the scheduling lead's rationale ('easier to present') as an adequate justification without weighing the cost to schedule integrity.
Treating this as a minor stylistic/formatting issue rather than a substantive quality and potential misrepresentation issue.
Focusing only on the technical CPM mechanics without addressing the reporting/ethical dimension of deliberately concealing real project variance from the client.
redFlags: Approves the submission without requiring any change once the rationale is explained.
Cannot articulate why a Mandatory-constraint-locked schedule cannot function as a genuine forecast.
p6Checks: Global filter for Mandatory Start/Finish constraints and export the list of 340 flagged activities for review.
Compare current actual progress against the constrained (frozen) dates to quantify how far the true, logic-driven picture has diverged from what is being shown.
Review the schedule submission history to determine how long this practice has been occurring and whether prior submissions to the client were similarly affected.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate holds the line on integrity while also managing the communication/change consequence responsibly.

skill: Distinguishing a project-level deadline setting from an activity-level date constraint and choosing the appropriate one
scenario: A new planner asks why the project uses a 'Finish On or Before' constraint on the project finish milestone to represent the contract completion date, instead of simply typing the contract date into the project's 'Must Finish By' field in the Project Details.
question: Explain the practical difference between an activity-level constraint (such as Finish On or Before on the finish milestone) and a project-level deadline setting (such as P6's Must Finish By field), and when you would use each.
expectedAnswer: A project-level Must Finish By date in P6 acts on the WHOLE PROJECT's backward pass, effectively capping the Late Finish of every path in the network relative to that single date (it is essentially a project-wide deadline applied globally), whereas an activity-level Finish On or Before constraint applies only to the specific activity or milestone it is placed on, only affecting that activity's own Late Finish (and, through the backward pass, its predecessors along that path). In practice, both can be used to represent a contract completion date, but placing the constraint directly on a dedicated finish milestone gives clearer visibility (a single named activity explicitly shows the deadline and its float relative to it, which is easier to explain to non-planners and easier to audit) while the project-level Must Finish By field is a more global setting that is less visible unless someone specifically checks Project Details, and can be easy to overlook or forget is set when reviewing the schedule.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate notes that using a dedicated activity/milestone-level constraint is generally the more transparent, auditable, and commonly recommended practice specifically because it appears directly in the Activities view like any other date, whereas the project-level setting is a background configuration that a schedule reviewer might not think to check, making it easier to miss.
expertAnswer: An expert notes both approaches mathematically achieve a similar capping effect on the backward pass, but flags that using BOTH simultaneously (a Must Finish By project setting plus a duplicate constraint on the milestone) risks confusion about which one is actually governing float displays, and recommends standardizing on one approach across the organization's schedules (most commonly the milestone-level constraint) for consistency and clarity across all project schedules and reviewers.
explanation: Both mechanisms can represent a contractual deadline in CPM terms, but they differ in scope (project-wide setting versus a single activity) and, more importantly, in visibility/auditability to a schedule reviewer, which is why most planning practice favors the explicit milestone-level constraint.
reasoning: The Must Finish By field is a project-configuration-level input that affects the backward pass globally without appearing as a visible date on any individual activity row, while a milestone constraint is an ordinary, visible activity attribute that any reviewer opening the Activities view and looking at that milestone's Constraints tab will immediately see, which is the core practical distinction driving the usual preference.
commonMistakes: Believing the two mechanisms are functionally identical in every respect, including visibility, rather than just in their date-capping effect.
Not recognizing the risk of using both simultaneously and losing track of which one is actually governing.
Assuming a project-level deadline setting is inherently more 'correct' or authoritative than an activity-level constraint, when in practice either can represent the same contractual fact.
redFlags: Cannot articulate any practical difference between the two mechanisms beyond 'they both make the date later'.
p6Checks: Project Details - Dates tab, check whether Must Finish By is populated.
Activities view - check the project finish milestone's Constraints tab for a Finish On or Before constraint.
If both are present, confirm with the scheduling team which one is intended to be the authoritative deadline representation.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests practical conflict-resolution when the two mechanisms disagree.

subcategory: Constraint Impact on Float and Critical Path
skill: Diagnosing how scattered unnecessary Finish On or Before constraints across intermediate activities suppress float and obscure the true critical path
scenario: A subcontractor submits a 900-activity pipe rack installation schedule showing the project finishing 40 days ahead of the contract completion date, with an unusually flat, uniform Total Float distribution: nearly every activity across every WBS area shows between 2 and 6 days of float, with no clear single critical path standing out. Investigation reveals that 210 intermediate activities (not just the project finish milestone) each carry an individually-applied Finish On or Before constraint, most set a few days apart from each other, roughly tracking what appears to be an internal target schedule built activity by activity.
question: Explain how scattering Finish On or Before constraints across many intermediate activities like this produces the flat, uniformly-low-float pattern observed, and why this makes the schedule's claimed critical path unreliable even though every individual date still 'calculates'.
explanation: Each individually-applied Finish On or Before constraint caps that specific activity's own Late Finish independently of the others, which means every one of those 210 activities gets its own artificially tight backward-pass boundary rather than deriving its Late Finish honestly from the genuine downstream logic chain leading to the real project finish - the result is that float is being calculated relative to 210 different local targets instead of one coherent network-wide critical path, which is exactly why the float distribution looks flat and uniform (each constraint is individually 'tight' by design) rather than showing the normal pattern of one or a few genuinely critical chains with zero/low float and the rest of the network carrying its real, often much higher, float. The '40 days ahead of contract' headline and the uniformly-low float are therefore not evidence of genuine schedule health; they are an artifact of scattered date-forcing that has replaced the network's real logic-driven critical path with 210 independently-imposed local deadlines, making it effectively impossible to tell from Total Float alone which activities are genuinely driving the finish date and which merely have a tight but arbitrary constraint.
reasoning: Total Float and the identification of the critical path both depend on Late Finish being derived consistently, network-wide, from actual logic back from the true project finish; once many individual activities each have their own independently-set Finish On or Before constraint, their Late Finish (and therefore their float) is decoupled from genuine downstream logic and instead reflects whatever date each constraint happens to specify, which can make even genuinely non-critical, high-float work appear tight, while genuinely critical work elsewhere may appear to have artificial slack if its own local constraint happens to be looser than its real logic-driven requirement.
commonMistakes: Accepting the '40 days ahead of schedule' headline at face value without investigating why the float distribution looks unusually uniform.
Assuming a flat, low, evenly-distributed float pattern is simply what a 'tight, well-managed' schedule looks like, rather than recognizing it as a classic symptom of pervasive constraint misuse.
Fixing this by removing only the project-level or most obviously excessive constraints, without recognizing the systemic nature of the problem across all 210 activities.
redFlags: Reports the 40-day favorable variance to management without investigating the constraint pattern behind it.
Cannot explain why a uniformly flat float distribution across hundreds of unrelated activities is itself suspicious.
p6Checks: Global filter/export for all Finish On or Before (and other) constraints, count and list every activity carrying one, not just a sample.
Temporarily remove all non-milestone Finish On or Before constraints in a working copy of the schedule and recalculate to reveal the genuine logic-driven critical path and float distribution.
Compare the genuine (constraint-free) critical path and finish date against the originally reported '40 days ahead' figure to quantify how much of that favorable variance was real versus artifact.

skill: Computing the percentage of activities carrying hard constraints as a schedule quality screening metric

subcategory: Constraint Types - Start On vs Mandatory Start
skill: Distinguishing Start On from Mandatory Start based on how each responds when predecessor logic would push the date later
scenario: Two nearly identical activities, 'Deliver Switchgear - Panel A' and 'Deliver Switchgear - Panel B', both originally had a predecessor-driven Early Start of Day 100 and were each given a fixed date constraint of Day 95, five days earlier than logic alone would produce, to reflect an agreed early-delivery slot with the supplier. Panel A was given a Start On constraint; Panel B was given a Mandatory Start constraint, both dated Day 95. Later, a change adds a new predecessor relationship to each panel's delivery activity that pushes its logic-driven Early Start to Day 110.
question: After the new predecessor relationship is added, what Early Start would you expect for Panel A (Start On) versus Panel B (Mandatory Start), and why do they now differ?
expectedAnswer: Panel A (Start On) would be expected to show an Early Start of Day 110: Start On respects predecessor logic when that logic pushes the date LATER than the constraint, so once the new relationship makes Day 110 the logic-driven date, that later date takes over. Panel B (Mandatory Start) would still show an Early Start fixed at Day 95, completely ignoring the new predecessor relationship, because Mandatory constraints override predecessor logic entirely regardless of whether logic would push the date earlier or later than the constraint.
strongAnswer: A strong candidate notes this exact scenario is why Mandatory constraints are considered dangerous in a live, evolving schedule: a new relationship added months later by someone unaware of the Mandatory constraint on Panel B will have silently no effect on that activity's calculated date, which could easily go unnoticed during a routine review.
expertAnswer: An expert recommends a standing schedule-quality control specifically for this failure mode: whenever a new relationship is added to an activity, check whether that activity carries a Mandatory constraint, since only then does the relationship risk being silently ignored - and suggests periodically filtering for and re-justifying every Mandatory constraint in the live schedule as new logic accumulates around it over the project's life.
explanation: The defining practical difference between Start On and Mandatory Start is what happens when predecessor logic would otherwise produce a LATER date than the constraint: Start On yields to the later logic-driven date, while Mandatory Start ignores predecessor logic entirely and holds the fixed date regardless.
reasoning: Start On behaves as a constraint that pins the date only up to the point where predecessor logic does not conflict with it in the later direction; if logic drives the date later, P6 uses the later logic-driven date since Start On does not suppress predecessor-driven pushes. Mandatory Start, by contrast, is excluded from the normal forward-pass logic propagation entirely, so it remains fixed at Day 95 no matter what any predecessor relationship, existing or newly added, would otherwise calculate.
commonMistakes: Believing Start On and Mandatory Start behave identically in every situation because both fix a date.
Assuming both would show Day 110 after the new relationship is added, not recognizing Mandatory Start's complete disregard for logic.
Assuming both would remain fixed at Day 95, not recognizing that Start On does respect a later logic-driven push.
redFlags: Cannot articulate any behavioral difference between Start On and Mandatory Start.
p6Checks: Activity Details - Constraints tab, confirm constraint type on each panel activity before and after adding the new relationship.
Recalculate the schedule after adding the new predecessor relationship and compare the two activities' resulting Early Start values directly.
Check for a 'constraint not satisfied' or similar flag/report that some P6 configurations surface for Start On when logic overrides it, versus the silence typical of Mandatory constraints.
